papers.abstract: Systems in which the free energy density is nonuniform in space are familiar: the surface tension of a water droplet and the surface energy of a solid are good examples. Some such cases can be treated with prior theory, notably inhomogeneous solvation theory (IST), but IST is applicable only to liquids. Despite this limitation, IST has proven useful as a guide to the design of ligands to bind a targeted protein, based on the idea that ligands which displace water at high free energy will tend to bind more tightly, {\em ceteris paribus}. Here, we present Generalized Thermodynamic Mapping Theory (GTMT), a more general theory that is applicable to the entirety of a biomolecular or other chemical system, and which thus may provide additional guidance for molecular design. For example, it might highlight parts of a ligand whose local free energy rises on binding, thus suggesting where modifications could improve affinity. Starting from classical statistical thermodynamics, we derive structural decompositions that assign energy and entropy to individual atoms or to larger chemical components such as amino acid residues, and spatial decompositions that define continuously varying thermodynamic densities throughout the system. The potential energy is decomposed via the multibody expansion, and the entropy via the mutual information expansion. The resulting thermodynamic densities satisfy key desiderata: their spatial integrals yield the correct total thermodynamic quantities, the densities vanish where the atomic number density is zero, and all entropy terms above first order go to zero in the absence of correlation. The entropy decomposition in GTMT is closely related to that of IST, but it is simpler, largely because it expresses the entropy in terms of normalized probability density functions instead of non-normalized correlation functions. We show that, while GTMT is formally exact for any number of particles, N, IST is formally inexact for finite N, although it becomes exact in the thermodynamic limit. The unified framework presented here enables thermodynamic mapping of solute and solvent alike and is expected to support a range of applications, including in structure-based drug design, protein design, the analysis of allostery, and materials science.

papers.title: Complexing Ligands Initiating the Silver Mirror Reaction at the Air–Liquid Interface
papers.abstract: Free-standing metal films represent a transformative platform for next-generation flexible electronics, energy storage, optoelectronics, and bio-integrated devices, offering unparalleled mechanical compliance unattainable with rigid substrates. However, the scalable synthesis of robust, large-area free-standing films via liquid-surface assembly remains a formidable challenge. Existing approaches, such as solid-liquid interface shielding (SLIS), often yield films that are intrinsically brittle and mechanically fragile, severely limiting their utility in practical wearable bioelectronics. Here, we report a trace-complex-agent-mediated liquid-level catalysis (TCALC) strategy that orchestrates the spontaneous growth of high-quality, self-supporting metal films at the gas-liquid interface. By introducing trace amounts (ppm-level) of specific complexing ligands into the reduction system, we precisely modulate the interfacial energy landscape to direct heterogeneous nucleation exclusively to the liquid surface, thereby bypassing bulk precipitation. Guided by a rational molecular screening mechanism, we demonstrate the universality of this approach across 21 distinct ligand families, enabling the fabrication of continuous silver films with tunable thicknesses up to 15 μm. These films exhibit exceptional electrical stability and mechanical resilience, serving as the foundational layer for breathable, ultra-comfortable Ag/AgCl bioelectrodes that meet the rigorous demands of long-term physiological monitoring. This work establishes a general, scalable paradigm for interfacial material synthesis, bridging the gap between delicate nanomaterials and robust industrial applications.

papers.title: Metal-Oxide Nanoparticles with Multipolar Cog-Wheel Coupling form Dynamic Mixtures of 2D Sheets and Self-Healable Hollow Vesicles
papers.abstract: The controlled self-assembly of inorganic nanocrystals (NCs) into dynamic architectures remains a central challenge in nanomaterials chemistry. Polyoxometalates (POMs) are known to form "blackberry" assemblies, with sheet-like structures proposed as their lower-symmetry precursors. Nevertheless, direct observation of both structural types within a single system has not been documented. We here show that when the protons are used as the POM countercations for the average of 10 [α-PW₁₁O₃₉Sn)] 3-O-Keggin-ion derived donor ligands to 3.6 ± 0.9 nm SnO₂ NCs, the surfaces of the NCs are extensively protonated by 33 ± 1 H + ions, giving complexed NCs with net charges of 7-± 1. The positively charged surface regions engage in "cog-wheel" like electrostatic interactions with polyanionic [PW₁₁O₃₉SnO]⁴⁻ ligands of neighbouring NCs, resulting in the assembly of 2D sheets observed by cryo-TEM imaging in the same solutions as symmetry-adopted hollow vesicles. Atomistic molecular-dynamics simulations confirm that protonated surface regions on one NC form favorable interactions with the anionic POM ligands of neighboring NCs with distances between ligands on the surfaces of both NCs stabilizing over time, with the persistence of interfacial ligand contacts proving the existence of a locking mechanism in these NCs. These findings introduce localized structural recognition as an operative control element in the electrostatic assembly of metal-oxide NCs.

papers.title: Benchmarking the UMA Foundation Interatomic Potential for Gas-Phase Chemical Kinetics
papers.abstract: Foundation machine-learned interatomic potentials promise rapid access to highquality potential energy surfaces, but their fitness for gas-phase chemical kinetics remains largely untested. Here we benchmark the Universal Models for Atoms (UMA) foundation model for gas-phase kinetics applications relevant to combustion and atmospheric chemistry using our automated KinBot workflow across 12 representative systems. We compare optimized structures and ZPE-corrected energetics against the parent level of theory, ωB97M-V/def2-TZVPD, and assess pathway discovery, stationarypoint fidelity, and downstream kinetic inputs such as conformer ordering and onedimensional hindered rotor scans. UMA reliably identifies the expected reaction channels over broad regions of chemical space, including pathways that are also a challenge for ab initio methods. Single-point DFT corrections at UMA geometries are an efficient way to improve energies. Overall, we suggest a practical hybrid workflow in which UMA performs inexpensive exploration and sampling, while DFT refinement is reserved for the important regions of the PES. Our results indicate that UMA can substantially accelerate rate coefficient calculations for gas-phase systems, motivating future work on uncertainty quantification, targeted finetuning, and ∆-learning corrections toward a gas-phase kinetics-specialized foundation model.

papers.title: Performance of machine learning tools for NMR crystallography
papers.abstract: Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) crystallography is a robust method for structure determination, but its reliance on density functional theory (DFT) for geometry refinement and tensor prediction limits its speed. While Machine Learning (ML) tools like ShiftML3 can predict magnetic shielding in seconds, they still require high-quality geometries typically produced by slow DFT optimizations. This study demonstrates that Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) eliminate this bottleneck for organic crystals by generating accurate structures without DFT calculations. Using the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA), we produced structural models that rival hybrid-DFT accuracy. Magnetic shielding predictions derived from these models are statistically indistinguishable from DFT benchmarks. The UMA-ShiftML3 workflow therefore serves as a proper "drop-in" replacement for conventional DFT-based refinement, enabling high-throughput NMR crystallography at dramatically reduced computational cost. Furthermore, by combining NMR sensitivity enhancement via Dynamic Nuclear Polarization (DNP) with these ML-based methods, we used extracted chemical shift tensors for L-histidine without isotopic enrichment that aid rapid discrimination between two polymorphs. While 13 C/ 15 N tensors alone are similar for the two polymorphs, incorporating 1 H chemical shift analysis enables discrimination between the monoclinic and orthorhombic forms. These results show how data-driven modeling and DNP can enable fast, accurate NMR crystallography at scale.

papers.title: Can Bioelectrocatalytic Films With Open Boundaries Confine Redox Cofactors?
papers.abstract: Electrochemically driven enzyme cascades require efficient transfer of intermediates and cofactors between enzymes. However, bioelectrocatalytic films have open boundaries, where diffusive loss across the film-solution interface may impede catalytic efficiency. By systematically exploring the parameter space, we identify the precise conditions that allow such films to confine redox cofactors. Counterintuitively, confinement in electrochemical films arises not from the mere local proximity of enzymes, but from the global interplay between cofactor reaction and diffusion. At steady state, confinement fundamentally results from reaction–diffusion boundary layers within the film, which isolate reactions from the film-electrolyte interface, dynamically trapping cofactors and intermediates even when open boundaries and large gradients provide a driving force for their diffusive loss to the electrolyte solution. Conversely, while confinement is not achievable under purely transient conditions, tuning cofactor reaction–diffusion kinetics yields order-of-magnitude increases in turnover numbers. These findings provide a general strategy for spatiotemporal control of intermediates and cofactors, broadly applicable beyond enzymatic reactions to diverse forms of heterogeneous cascade catalysis.

papers.title: Higher resolution relaxometry with pure-shift NMR
papers.abstract: High-resolution relaxometry (HRR) is an NMR method to investigate multiscale dynamics of chemical and biological systems, giving access to spin relaxation over orders of magnitude of magnetic field while maintaining the resolution and sensitivity of high-field NMR. We have recently shown that proton high-resolution relaxometry could identify transient interactions of small molecules with macromolecules in complex mixtures such as blood serum and recover atom-specific information. Yet, proton spectra of such mixtures can suffer from severe signal overlaps due to multiplet patterns from scalar couplings. Here, we introduce a pure shift-based experiment to measure site-specific longitudinal relaxation rates with enhanced resolution. We illustrate this pure-shift approach by detecting the differential binding of amino acids to a protein with a sample-shuttle system covering magnetic fields from 36 mT to 14.1 T installed on a conventional 600 MHz NMR spectrometer.

papers.title: Particle Interactions Govern Fractional Viscoelasticity in Granular Hydrogels
papers.abstract: Granular hydrogels have emerged over the past decade as versatile biomaterials with applications ranging from tissue engineering to 3D bioprinting. Despite their widespread use, how particle-level interactions govern their collective mechanical dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigate how the properties of PEGDA microgels determine the rheological behavior of their jammed assemblies using oscillatory shear rheology. We develop a fractional rheology model that captures the frequency-dependent response of these materials, revealing distinct power-law behavior across frequency regimes and the presence of a dominant relaxation process. To probe the role of interparticle interactions, we implement an amide-coupling strategy to PEGylate microgel surfaces and thereby tune their tribological properties. PEGylation produces a nonmonotonic modification of the strain–stress response and systematically alters the power-law mechanical behavior. In particular, increasing interparticle lubrication markedly reduces the peak relaxation modulus without significantly shifting the characteristic relaxation time, indicating that these features are governed by distinct physical mechanisms. Within the fractional rheology framework, we further show that the fractional parameter β is directly linked to particle interactions, providing experimental evidence that this parameter reflects tangible microscopic properties. Together, these results establish a direct connection between microscopic particle interactions and macroscopic rheological response, and suggest a general strategy for engineering the mechanics of granular hydrogels through surface chemistry.

papers.title: Polyurea Molecular Layer Deposition using Low Melting Point Precursors for Use in Biosensor Design
papers.abstract: Molecular layer deposition (MLD) is a promising tool that could replace silane-based self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) in some surface functionalization applications, such as in biosensor design where a multilayer film is acceptable and a precise, conformal film thickness is desirable. This work presents an unexplored polyurea MLD chemistry using 2,4-toluene diisocyanate (TDIC) and ethylene diamine (ED). This process has some benefits over the similar and more common 1,4-phenylene diisocyanate (PDIC) precursor, such as reduced cost and lower melting point (and thus higher vapor pressure at room temperature). Film characterization suggests that this process is similarly well-behaved to PDIC-based polyurea: in situ ellipsometry shows that the process is both linear up to 55 cycles and self-saturating, XPS analysis shows the expected atomic ratio of oxygen and nitrogen in the film, and FTIR shows amide I & II peaks characteristic of polyurea. In addition, the films were analyzed using zeta potential analysis, fluorescence tagging, and water contact angle (WCA) goniometry to characterize their suitability for use in biosensor design.

papers.title: Pure Hydrocarbon Emitter with 6 nm FWHM
papers.abstract: High-purity emitters with an ultranarrow-band emission are a critical requirement for next-generation displays and lighting, yet it remains a formidable challenge for purely organic materials, particularly in the ultraviolet region. Herein, a general molecular design strategy based on the "stereo-lock" concept, represented by diarylbenzene derivatives solely from carbon and hydrogen, is presented. This strategy effectively suppresses intramolecular C-C/C-H stretching and attenuates vibronic coupling via intramolecular through-space interactions between two aryl groups, yielding a record full width at half maximum (FWHM) of merely 6 nm at 80 K from a single molecule. In the solid state, their aggregates with intermolecular positive exciton coupling induce quantum interference that selectively quenches the v 0-0 transition, resulting in an ultranarrow FWHM of 17 nm at room temperature. Leveraging this synergy, diarylbenzene-based OLED devices with pure ultraviolet electroluminescence with an 18 nm FWHM and a CIE coordinate of (0.165, 0.022) are achieved. This stereo-lock architecture circumvents the fundamental limitation of vibronic coupling in pure hydrocarbons and addresses the absence of high-color-purity ultraviolet OLEDs, establishing a powerful and versatile design paradigm for narrowband emitters.

papers.title: Synthesis and characterization of monomeric, dimeric and polymeric rare earth bis(trimethyl)silylphosphide complexes
papers.abstract: Rare earth (RE) bis(trimethylsilyl)amide ({N(SiMe3)2} − , Nʹʹ) chemistry is well-developed, but there are few examples of RE complexes containing the analogous phosphide ligand, {P(SiMe3)2} − (Pʹʹ). Here we report the synthesis and characterization of a series of dimeric RE Pʹʹ complexes, [RE(Pʹʹ)2(μ-Pʹʹ)]2 (1-RE; RE = Y, Gd, Dy, Er) by separate protonolysis reactions between parent [RE(CH2C6H4-o-NMe2)3] and 3.3 equivalents of HPʹʹ; the synthesis of 1-Y was previously reported by a different route. The reactions of 1-RE with four equivalents of THF gave the corresponding THF-solvated monomeric RE Pʹʹ complexes [RE(Pʹʹ)3(THF)2] (2-RE; RE = Y, Gd, Dy, Er), and treatment of 1-RE with two equivalents of KPʹʹ gave the RE 'ate' coordination polymers [RE(Pʹʹ)2(μ-Pʹʹ)2K]∞ (3-RE; Y, Gd, Dy, Er). Complexes 1-RE, 2-RE and 3-RE were characterized by single crystal XRD, elemental analysis, and NMR, ATR-IR and UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy. All paramagnetic 1-RE and 2-RE were also characterized by EPR spectroscopy and SQUID magnetometry, and these data were benchmarked by ab initio calculations. We find that weak magnetic exchange interactions persist between RE centers in dimeric 1-RE, and that their principal magnetic axes are oriented between the phosphide ligands as a consequence of the diffuse crystal field associated with the long REP bonds. For monomeric 2-RE the principal magnetic axes are also oriented between ligands, reflecting competition between three long REP bonds and two short RE-O bonds that contribute approximately equally to the crystal field anisotropy.

papers.title: Innate Chiroselectivity in the Formation of Pabmaragramin, a Scalemic Natural Product
papers.abstract: Natural products have long played a crucial role in drug discovery. Their complex three-dimensional structures result in potent and highly selective biological activities. The absolute configuration of these compounds is essential for their function. They typically exist as enantiopure compounds when formed through enzymatic biosynthesis, while nonenzymatic pathways often produce racemic mixtures. The occurrence of scalemic natural products – those isolated in moderate enantiomeric excess – challenge this binary logic. One such natural product is pabmaragramin, a metabolite from the Marasmius graminum fungus, isolated in an enantiomeric ratio of 65:35. Both enantiomers of pabmaragramin exhibit similar α-glucosidase inhibitory activity, but their full antihyperglycemic potential remains unexplored. Here, we report a four-step total synthesis of pabmaragramin, providing access to practical quantities of this complex natural product in both racemic and enantioenriched forms. Central to this synthesis is an intricate biomimetic cascade reaction featuring a Diels-Alder dimerization that exhibits innate chiroselectivity ( i.e. , homochiral versus heterochiral selectivity). Computational studies offer insights into the factors driving this rare case of homochiral selectivity, which may help address the emerging challenge of chiroselectivity in synthesis. This work highlights the potential of scalemic natural products to inspire advances in synthetic chemistry, offering novel opportunities through their unique biochemistry.

papers.title: PLANT LEAF EXTRACTS AS GREEN CORROSION INHIBITORS : A COMPARATIVE REVIEW
papers.abstract: The phenomenon of corrosion of metals when placed in acidic environments is one of the greatest obstacles for the industries and thus have been attempted to solve by the use of certain corrosion inhibitors. Many of them are synthetic chemicals that can be harmful to the environment. Because of this concern, researchers have increasingly focused on plant-based substances as safer and more sustainable alternatives. This review summarizes and compares the use of different plant leaf extracts as green corrosion inhibitors, mainly for mild steel in acidic solutions. Many of these extracts contain natural phytochemicals such as flavonoids, tannins, alkaloids and terpenoids, which can adsorb on metal surfaces and form a protective layer that slows down corrosion. Previous studies show that several leaf extracts demonstrate high inhibition efficiencies, often above 90%. The findings indicate that plant leaves are a promising, environmentally friendly source of corrosion inhibitors and could serve as practical alternatives to conventional chemical inhibitors in industrial applications.

papers.title: Time-Quasicrystals Dynamically Protected Topological Phases in Driven Dissipative Systems
papers.abstract: The classification of phases of matter has been revolutionised by topological order and nonequilibrium phenomena such as time crystals. However, a unified framework connecting temporal order, topology, and dissipation remains elusive. Here we introduce the concept of "Time-Quasicrystals"-non-equilibrium topological phases that exhibit quasi-periodic temporal order protected by dissipative dynamics. These phases emerge in driven dissipative quantum systems through the interplay of Floquet engineering and non-local dissipation, leading to an effective non-Hermitian Floquet Hamiltonian with topological edge modes in the frequency domain. We demonstrate three hallmarks of Time-Quasicrystals: (1) fractal-like temporal correlations with multiple incommensurate frequencies, (2) a quantised topological invariant robust against disorder, and (3) algebraically decaying memory of phase perturbations. We provide explicit experimental realisations in Rydberg atom arrays and circuit quantum electrodynamics platforms. Our work establishes Time-Quasicrystals as a bridge between topological phases, time crystals, and quantum simulation, opening pathways to dissipativeprotected quantum memory and novel non-equilibrium quantum phenomena.

papers.title: Vinylsiloxanes as Alkenylating Agents in Nickel-Catalyzed Difunctionalization of Vinylarenes
papers.abstract: Intermolecular nickel-catalyzed alkene difunctionalization has emerged as a powerful platform for rapidly increasing molecular complexity from simple olefin feedstocks. Although alkylation and arylation variants are well-established, three-component alkenylation reactions, that directly install synthetically versatile alkenyl motifs remain underdeveloped. Existing approaches typically rely on directing groups, exhibit narrow substrate scope, and require moisture-sensitive organometallic reagents. Herein, we report the first directing-group-free nickel-catalyzed three-component difunctionalization of vinylarenes using bench-stable vinylsiloxanes as stereodefined alkenylating agents. This mild and scalable protocol delivers regioselective access to densely functionalized disubstituted alkenes with low catalyst loadings, broad electrophile compatibility and excellent functional group tolerance. Diverse alkene geometries are accommodated with minimal Z -isomerization. By unlocking organosilicon reagents as alkenyl transfer partners, this strategy expands the conceptual and practical scope of alkene difunctionalization and establishes vinylsiloxanes as versatile synthetic linchpins in multicomponent nickel catalysis

papers.title: Thionation-Enhanced Through-Space Electronic Coupling and Excited-State Dynamics in Helicene Diimides
papers.abstract: Helicene diimides (HDIs) provide a unique platform in which electronic communication between redox centers is governed not only by through-bond conjugation but also by pronounced through-space interactions. While thionation is known to enhance electronic coupling in planar rylene diimides, its impact on intramolecular through-space charge transfer in nonplanar π-systems remains unexplored. Here, we report the synthesis of a fully thionated [8]helicene diimide ([8]HDI_S4) and a comparative study with its oxo analogue ([8]HDI_O4). Spectroelectrochemical analysis of the mixed-valence states reveals a substantial increase in electronic coupling (V12 = 2921 vs 1346 cm-1), moving the system toward the Robin-Day Class II/III boundary and indicating enhanced charge delocalization between the imide units. Ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy demonstrates accelerated charge-transfer formation and solvent-dependent dynamics, while nanosecond measurements reveal strongly shortened triplet lifetimes consistent with enhanced spin-orbit coupling. Together, these results show that thionation amplifies intramolecular throughspace electronic coupling and profoundly alters excited-state pathways in HDIs, establishing a general design principle for tuning charge-transfer processes in chiral three-dimensional organic semiconductors.

papers.title: Remote Asymmetric ε-or η-Position Substitution Reactions of Naphthalene-Blocked Alkynes
papers.abstract: Achieving asymmetric remote ε/η-position substitution of alkynes at sites far from the catalytic center poses considerable challenges, due to the requirements for high complexity, diverse structures and precise stereocontrol. To tackle this challenge, novel yne-naphthalene esters were developed using a naphthalene ring spacer and alkynyl coppermediated electron transfer, remote leaving group cleavage enabled asymmetric remote ε/η-arylation with 5-aminopyrazoles, affording diarylmethyl/triarylmethyl products in high yields with good to excellent enantioselectivities for the first time. Additionally, a gram-scale experiment and further derivatizations of chiral remote ε/η-arylation of yne-naphthalene esters were performed to validate the practicability of the methodology and the potential transformations of the products. Finally, control experiments, nonlinear effects, UV absorption spectra, and Job's plot further validated the scientific rationality of our proposed mechanism. Meanwhile, DFT calculations suggest that N-H ... π interactions were found to play a key role in the stereoselective control.

papers.title: Mixing of Spacer Cations in 2D Halide Perovskites
Foundation model distillation with PiNNAcLe: application to the ZnCl2 aqueous electrolyte solution
papers.abstract: Aqueous zinc chloride solutions are central to zinc-based electrochemical energy storage and electrochemical sensors, yet their local structure and dynamics remain challenging to characterize without atomistic simulation. Foundation models for materials chemistry can substantially accelerate such simulations, but they often impose significantly higher computational overhead than bespoke machine-learning interatomic potential. Here we bridge these two regimes by developing a workflow that distils a foundation model into our lightweight PiNet2 architecture, enabled by an extension of PiNNAcLe (Pair-wise Interaction Neural Network with Active Learn-on-the-fly). We demonstrate the approach for ZnCl2 (aq), and show that the framework can seamlessly switch between two foundation models at different density functional theory levels. Structural and dynamical properties from the distilled models have been validated against the foundation models as well as the density functional theory-based molecular dynamics simulations at matched levels of theory. This work provides a model-agnostic route to harnessing foundation models with low-cost bespoke models, enabling routine, scalable simulations of electrolyte systems.

papers.title: Zwitterionic Photoswitches for Dynamic Hydrogen-Bond Pairing
papers.abstract: Forming discrete hydrogen-bond pairs is a powerful strategy used to achieve highly selective chemical transformations and functions. Although the development of such noncovalent complexes has expanded rapidly over the past several decades, systems that deliberately form reversible, discrete hydrogen-bond pairs remain limited. We report a new class of zwitterionic Stenhouse photoswitches with intrinsic hydrogen-bond-accepting capabilities. Leveraging highly inductive sulfonyl groups, the ring-opening rearrangement of N-sulfonyl pyrrole-2carboxaldehydes provides isolable streptocyanine zwitterions that form hydrogen-bond pairs with fluorinated alcohols. Upon visible light irradiation, the chromophoric hydrogen-bond acceptor isomerizes to a colorless cyclic adduct with up to 96% efficiency, simultaneously releasing the paired hydrogen-bond donor. A direct correlation between triene electronic structure, photoswitching efficiency, and hydrogen-bonding capacity demonstrates the tunability of this platform for future spatiotemporally activated applications.

papers.title: Quantum Assembly Theory: Bridging QTAIM and Molecular Complexity via Electron Density Topology
Magnetic fields from microscopic sources: a new quantum-based discrete interaction approach
papers.abstract: At nanometer scales, the Ørsted magnetic field generated by electrical current no longer strictly follows continuum magnetostatics. A nitrogen–vacancy magnetometry experiment reported suppressed and spatially reshaped magnetic fields in metallic nanowires, and these deviations are not captured by the Biot–Savart law. We introduce a microscopic current–magnetisation (CMH) framework that reconstructs magnetic induction directly from electron–ion correlations within atomically resolved conductors. Each carrier generates a locally screened axial source determined by its motion relative to nearby ions, yielding an exactly divergence-free magnetic field through a compact vector-potential formulation. The Biot–Savart kernel emerges only as a long-distance coarse-grained limit. When device dimensions approach the screening length, CMH predicts intrinsic field suppression and spatial smoothing. Crucially, the framework enables direct prediction of molecular orbital ring-current fields, revealing near-field structures that differ qualitatively from continuum loop models while preserving correct long-range behavior. CMH reframes current-induced magnetism at the atomic scale, where classical approaches fail, and opens a new and predictive pathway for engineering magnetic responses to enable design of next-generation nanomagnetic devices with improved performance.

papers.title: Decoding Chemical Resonance in π-Conjugated Systems
papers.abstract: Understanding the electronic structure of (anti)aromatic poly- and macrocyclic π-conjugated systems remains a central challenge in contemporary chemistry, given their importance in materials science, molecular electronics, photophysics, and catalysis. While magnetically induced ring currents and NMR-based descriptors have long served as key indicators of (anti)aromatic character, the extent to which such magnetic observables reflect the full ground-state π-bonding architecture becomes less transparent in large and topologically complex systems. Here we introduce a wavefunction-based analytical protocol — the π-Bond Delocalization Function (BDFπ) — which maps the spatial organization of localized and delocalized π-bonding directly from the ground-state one-electron density matrix. Rather than relying on predefined resonance models or orbital localization schemes, the method extracts bonding topology from the complete occupied π-space. This enables a direct comparison between the global π-electron distribution and the more selective subset of frontier-orbital excitations that dominate magnetic response phenomena. Applied to representative poly- and macrocyclic systems frequently discussed in the context of global (anti)aromaticity, BDFπ reveals that magnetic ring currents and bonding delocalization need not coincide quantitatively in extended conjugated frameworks. Magnetic descriptors predominantly probe perturbative response channels, whereas the underlying resonance structure reflects the collective organization of the entire occupied π-manifold. By explicitly relating these two perspectives, the present framework provides a coherent and chemically transparent account of how resonance topology and experimentally observable magnetic behavior are connected — and where they may diverge — in large conjugated architectures.

papers.title: A Brief Study on Analysing Balanced Chemical Equations
papers.abstract: Balanced chemical equations are often considered endpoints, but the equations themselves exhibit patterns that can serve explanatory purposes. This study examines selected redox and acid–base neutralisation reactions to identify and clarify recurring relationships between coefficients. By comparing reactions within defined groups, common structural patterns become clearer and can help make the balancing process more intuitive. Although this work does not propose a new balancing method, it suggests that examining the structure of balanced equations may help students better understand how and why intuitive balancing methods work.

papers.title: Large-scale collaborative assessment of binding free energy calculations for drug discovery using OpenFE
papers.abstract: Accurately measuring compound binding affinities is key to driving the pharmaceutical development process. Rigorous physics-based in silico approaches, particularly alchemical free energy methods, have become a gold standard tool for estimating compound affinity changes. Here we present the results of a large-scale pre-competitive collaborative assessment of relative binding free energy (RBFE) calculations generated by 15 pharmaceutical companies. We evaluate an open-source and MIT licensed RBFE Protocol from the Open Free Energy (OpenFE) ecosystem across both public and blinded private datasets, encompassing over 1,700 ligands in total. For the public dataset, the weighted RMSE across the 58 systems was 1.73 [1.53, 1.96] kcal/mol, with 10 of the systems reaching sub-kcal/mol accuracy. For the private dataset, the weighted RMSE across the 37 systems was 2.44 [1.94, 3.06] kcal/mol, with only 2 of the systems reaching sub-kcal/mol accuracy, reflecting the increased complexity of real-world drug discovery. The protocols performance was system-dependent, with no single dominant error source, indicating that accuracy is primarily influenced by input quality and transformation type. Overall, these benchmark results are encouraging and indicate that OpenFE is ready for large-scale industrial applications, with an "out-of-the-box" accuracy that approaches that of commercial solutions. While comparison against published FEP+ results, which were obtained after manual parameter optimization, shows comparable ranking statistics, a gap remains in error statistics, for which we outline possible paths toward improvement. The protocol meets key criteria required for production use in an industrial setting: it shows robust performance, generates reproducible results, and achieves both sufficient throughput and rapid convergence.

papers.title: Organocatalytic Aerobic Oxidative Monodealkylation of tert-Amines to sec-Amines
papers.abstract: The highly efficient monodealkylation of tertiary amines was achieved using hydroxylamine and NOx catalysts under mildly aerobic conditions. This approach demonstrates high functional group tolerance and a broad substrate scope, including amino acids and alkaloids with complex structures. Mechanistic studies have suggested that the reaction proceeds via aminium radical cations via the one-electron oxidation of tertiary amines.

papers.title: Structural Determinants of Prebiotic Carbohydrates and Their Impact on Gut Microbiota Fermentation
papers.abstract: Prebiotic carbohydrates have gained increasing attention due to their ability to selectively modulate the gut microbiota and promote host health. These non-digestible compounds reach the colon intact, where they are fermented by specific microbial populations, leading to the production of metabolites such as short-chain fatty acids that contribute to intestinal and systemic health. A variety of carbohydrate-based substrates exhibit prebiotic properties, including fructans, Galactooligosaccharides, Human Milk Oligosaccharides, Pectic oligosaccharides, Xylooligosaccharides, Arabinoxylans, Resistant starch and Polydextrose. Although these compounds differ considerably in their chemical composition and structural organization, their physiological effects are largely determined by microbial fermentation processes occurring in the gut microbiota. This review examines the structural determinants that govern the fermentability and microbiota modulation of carbohydrate-based prebiotics. Particular attention is given to the influence of glycosidic linkages, degree of polymerization, branching patterns, and molecular weight on microbial utilization and fermentation dynamics. Understanding these structure-function relationships is essential for the rational design of next-generation prebiotic ingredients aimed at targeted modulation of the gut microbiome.

papers.title: Near-Infrared-Absorbing Aminoxyl Radical-Boron Complexes with Reduced Visible Coloration
papers.abstract: We report the synthesis and optical properties of new aminoxyl radical-boron complexes bearing dimethylamino and methoxy substituents as electron-donating groups. The target cationic radical complexes were obtained by oxidation of the corresponding neutral aminoxide-boron precursors. Electron spin resonance spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations revealed that the nature of the electron-donating substituent influences the spin density distribution, promoting delocalization of the unpaired electron over the conjugated framework. The radical complexes exhibit intense absorption in the near-infrared (NIR) region, with absorption maxima at 1210 nm for the dimethylamino-substituted complex and 993 and 1080 nm for the methoxy-substituted complex. Compared with previously reported analogues bearing a diarylamino-type electron-donating group, the present complexes show reduced visible coloration owing to hypsochromic shifts of the secondary absorption bands in the visible region, resulting in improved visible transparency. These results demonstrate that substituent tuning provides an effective strategy for balancing strong NIR absorption with reduced visible coloration in aminoxyl radical-boron complexes.

papers.title: High Throughput Screening of Alucone and Zincone Extreme Ultraviolet Photoresists through Molecular Layer Deposition
papers.abstract: As extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography advances toward sub-10 nm half-pitch patterning, photoresists must deliver improved sensitivity while enabling higher resolution and reduced line-edge roughness. Hybrid organic-inorganic thin films deposited via molecular layer deposition (MLD) offer tunable composition and enhanced EUV absorptivity, making them promising resist candidates. Here, using a high-throughput MLD reactor, we screen twelve chemistries, comprising aluminum-and zinc-based hybrids linked by one of six organic diols, for their stability and processability. From these, an alkynefunctionalized alucone incorporating 2-butyne-1,4-diol (BTY) emerged as the leading candidate for detailed study. Characterization of this chemistry through Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, and time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry confirmed alkyne incorporation within the hybrid network, where the electron-rich triple bond may serve as a preferential site for radiation-induced crosslinking. Using electron-beam lithography at 100 kV as a proxy for EUV resist evaluation, a sensitivity of 𝐷 50 = 2695 µC cm −2 with high contrast, 𝛾 = 2.19, was achieved while requiring 300× more dilute developer than previously reported hafnium-based MLD resists. Compared to other aluminum-based MLD resists, BTY-alucone exhibited 21-33× higher sensitivity. Dense patterns at 20 nm half-pitch were also achieved. These results establish alkyne-functionalized alucone as a promising EUV resist candidate and validate high-throughput MLD screening for accelerated resist development.

papers.title: Manners of Dispersion-Corrected Density Functionals for Treating Dispersion Interactions from Short to Long Ranges
papers.abstract: Dispersion-corrected density functionals remedy the shortcomings of the corresponding uncorrected density functionals on noncovalent interactions. In this work, we have analyzed some widely used dispersion-corrected density functionals with the generalized Kohn-Sham energy decomposition analysis (GKS-EDA) method. Between two interacting subsystems, the sum of contributions from correlation component and dispersion correction for a dispersion-corrected density functional is only approximately comparable with the dispersion energy obtained with the symmetry-adapted perturbation theory (SAPT) from short to long ranges. The ratios of the correlation components to the SAPT dispersion energies are remarkably dependent on the interacting subsystems at short range. However, they are much more dependent on the exchange-correlation functionals at medium and long ranges. Specifically, the correlation components are significantly affected by the Hartree-Fock (HF) exchanges included in the hybrid density functionals.

papers.title: Chemical Composition and Antimicrobial Activity of the Essential Oil from Piper carpunya Ruiz & Pav. ("Guaviduca") Leaves
papers.abstract: The essential oil (EO) obtained from dried leaves of Piper carpunya Ruiz & Pav. ("Guaviduca") was isolated by hydrodistillation and characterized by GC-MS. The EO yield was 1.22% (v/w) from 180 g of dried leaves after 3 h of hydrodistillation, corresponding to 2.20 mL of oil. The refractive index and relative density were 1.49 and 0.95, respectively. GC-MS analysis identified compounds accounting for 97.52% of the total chromatographic area, with piperitone (40.35%) as the major constituent, followed by methyl eugenol (8.98%), sylvestrene (6.76%), d-limonene (6.30%), and 1,8-cineole/eucalyptol (6.29%). Antimicrobial activity was evaluated by disk diffusion using the pure EO against selected bacterial ATCC strains and clinical isolates of Candida. The EO showed limited antibacterial activity, with inhibition halos ranging from 6 to 10 mm against Escherichia coli ATCC 25922, Klebsiella pneumoniae ATCC 700603, Pseudomonas aeruginosa ATCC 27853, Staphylococcus aureus ATCC 25923, and Enterococcus faecalis ATCC 29212. In contrast, marked antifungal activity was observed against two clinical isolates of Candida albicans, Candida tropicalis, and Candida glabrata, with inhibition halos ranging from 34 to 42 mm. These results indicate that the EO of Piper carpunya displays predominantly antifungal rather than antibacterial activity under the conditions tested.

papers.title: UAC-GNN: Uncertainty-Aware Contrastive Graph Neural Networks for Left-Censored ADMET Property Prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate ADMET property prediction is crucial for drug discovery but is hampered by leftcensored data, which leads to biased models and performance degradation in existing graph neural networks. We propose the Uncertainty-Aware Contrastive Graph Neural Network (UAC-GNN), a novel framework that explicitly models censored label uncertainty and leverages contrastive learning on molecular pairs. UAC-GNN employs a D-MPNN encoder, differential representation learning, and a dual-branch prediction head for property differences and their associated uncertainties. An innovative uncertainty-aware contrastive loss combines Gaussian likelihood for observed data, an uncertainty boundary loss for censored data, and a triplet term to enforce relative relationships. Extensive experiments on 10 diverse ADMET datasets, including highly censored internal Merck data, show UAC-GNN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. It demonstrates superior robustness and accuracy, particularly under high censorship rates. Ablation studies confirm component contributions, and qualitative analysis highlights the utility of our uncertainty estimates. UAC-GNN provides a robust solution for accurate ADMET prediction in drug discovery.

papers.title: Chemical Space Exploration of a Database of Covalent Binders in the PDB
Target-Directed Stapled Peptides through Dynamic Combinatorial Chemistry
papers.abstract: Target-directed dynamic combinatorial chemistry (tdDCC) enables biological targets to assemble and amplify their preferred ligands from pools of reversibly interconverting fragments. Here, we report the application of this concept to the discovery of stapled peptides targeting protein-protein interactions. A cysteine-containing peptide was combined with a series of thioester-containing staple building blocks under physiological conditions, generating a dynamic combinatorial library of constrained peptides via reversible thioester exchange. Using the oncoprotein hDM2 as a template, the dynamic system selectively amplified the optimal stapled peptide targeting the p53-hDM2 interaction-a prominent target in cancer research. This work establishes tdDCC as a powerful platform for the discovery of stapled peptides and highlights the potential of dynamic combinatorial approaches to address challenging protein-protein interactions.

papers.title: Hollow UO2 Tetrapods via Single-Step Sacrificial Templating Unveiled by In Situ Electron Microscopy
papers.abstract: The ongoing global nuclear renaissance and expansion of nuclear power capacity demand advanced materials that enhance fuel performance, improve waste management, and enhance radiation resilience. Research on nuclear nanomaterials could help address such challenges. While uranium dioxide remains the archetypal nuclear fuel, its nanostructured morphologies remain largely unexplored beyond simple particles. Here, the family of nuclear nanomaterials was enlarged by new members, hollow tetrapodal and microtubular uranium dioxides. These nanostructures were formed through sacrificial templating using tetrapodal zinc oxide and a uranyl complex at elevated temperatures in a reducing atmosphere. While the uranyl complex initially decomposed, forming a shell of nanocrystalline UO 2 on the template surface, the ZnO tetrapods evaporated at elevated temperature, leaving hollow cavities. Synthesized materials were structurally and chemically analyzed by various techniques. Importantly, the mechanism and reaction conditions of material formation were investigated by advanced in situ imaging. Obtained tetrapodal UO 2 delivers low-density voluminous material that could find applications in heat shielding, an expedient sorbent of nuclear waste, or as a structure guiding additive to nuclear fuel forming sinks for fission gases.

papers.title: Enzyme-Polymer stickers for assembling single and multi-analyte biosensors
papers.abstract: Electrochemical biosensors have achieved widespread commercial success due to their high selectivity, ease of use, and low cost. However, the fabrication of many such systems, especially when targeting multianalyte sensing, is often constrained by the preparation of the sensing film, which typically relies on drop-casting a polymer–enzyme solutions followed by drying to form the active layer. Depending on the enzyme-polymer formulation, this step can be difficult to integrate into large-scale, roll-to-roll production processes and lacks flexibility for constructing multianalyte sensors. Here, we propose a new fabrication concept in which the sensing film is produced separately as transferable sensor stickers. These stickers contain enzymes and redox polymers and can be transferred in a single step either onto singular electrodes to generate single-analyte sensors or combined on electrode arrays for multianalyte sensing. We demonstrate the sensor sticker concept using four oxidoreductases as biorecognition elements that catalyze the oxidation or reduction of four different analytes (H₂, HCOONa, KNO₃, and NADPH). Accurate sensing was achieved on both standard glassy carbon electrodes and on specifically designed microelectrode arrays modified with the sensor stickers. The stickers exhibited high selectivity with minimal interference, even in mixed samples containing all four analytes. This modular approach to assembling multianalyte sensors on microarrays is broadly applicable to other analytes and holds strong promise for flexible, customizable, and scalable fabrication of multianalyte biosensors.

papers.title: Yb M5 -edge XMCD of molecular complexes: Can spin and orbital moments be resolved for YbPc2 ?
Bicarbonate liquid condensate controls manganese partitioning in calcite
papers.abstract: Crystals formed in aqueous solutions often encode chemical memories of their growth environment. However, the molecular pathway of element partitioning that links solution chemistry to solid composition remains elusive when growth proceeds through nonclassical intermediates. In this study, we investigated calcite growth mechanisms in the presence of aqueous manganese (Mn 2+ ) under chemostat conditions using a custom titration method. At near-neutral pH, where bicarbonate ions dominate, we show that Mn 2+ triggers the formation of bicarbonate-rich, ion-paired liquid condensates that accumulate at the calcite-water interface and control Mn incorporation. Time-resolved in situ X-ray scattering and Raman spectroscopy, combined with cryogenic transmission electron microscopy and molecular dynamics simulations, reveal a pathway in which these condensates deprotonate and dehydrate into Mn-bearing amorphous carbonate that crystallizes into polycrystalline calcite-rhodochrosite interfacial solid solutions with progressively increasing Mn content. These results identify an interfacial, bicarbonaterich liquid condensate as a mechanistic link between crystallization pathway and element partitioning, suggesting that nanoscale interfacial fluid organization can dominate selective ion uptake during mineralization in multicomponent aqueous environments that are relevant to geoscience, environmental science, chemistry or materials sciences.

papers.title: Zinc halide flux-assisted vitrification of metal-organic frameworks enables chemical diversification and tunable gas sorption
papers.abstract: The vitrification of metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) enables melt processing into bulk, shaped and membrane-type porous materials, yet the limited chemical diversity of existing MOF glass formers restricts structural and functional tunability. Here, we demonstrate a general flux-melting strategy in which the inorganic glass formers ZnBr 2 or ZnI 2 are co-melted with seven zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIFs) spanning different imidazolate-type linkers and network topologies, including both established ZIF glass formers and frameworks that do not melt or vitrify on their own. The zinc halides act as compatible co-network formers and reactive fluxes, promoting extensive ligand exchange between halides and imidazolate linkers in the melt. This process generates mixed halide-imidazolate coordination glass networks whose structure, connectivity and porosity can be tuned systematically through composition. One of the resulting hybrid glasses displays substantially enhanced thermodynamic sorption selectivity for propylene over propane compared to its parent ZIF glass. These results establish zinc-halide flux melting as a general route to expand the compositional space of MOF glasses and introduce mixed coordination networks as a new design paradigm for functional porous glasses.

papers.title: Complete Trajectory of a Charged Ion in Bounded Phase Space
papers.abstract: We trace the complete trajectory of a single ion (m/z = 299.0555) through a mass spectrometer, from electrospray ionization through chromatographic separation and mass analysis to detection.

papers.title: Partition Lagrangian Formulation of Ion Dynamics: A Unified Framework for Mass Analyzer Physics
papers.abstract: We develop a Lagrangian formulation of ion dynamics in mass spectrometers based on the principle of partition depth minimization. The framework introduces partition depth M(x, t) as the fundamental field governing ion motion, with ions interpreted as partition malformations seeking categorical completion at the detector. We derive the partition Lagrangian L M = 1 2 µ| ẋ| 2 +µ ẋ•A M −M(x, t), where µ = α(m/z) is the partition inertia. From this single Lagrangian, we derive the equations of motion for all major mass analyzer types: time-of-flight (T ∝ m/z), quadrupole (Mathieu stability parameters), Orbitrap (ω ∝ z/m), and Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance (ω c ∝ z/m). We establish the fundamental identity dM/dt = 1/⟨τ p ⟩ connecting temporal evolution to partition state counting, and derive the partition uncertainty relation ∆M•τ p ≥ ℏ, which yields the fundamental resolution limit [∆(m/z)/(m/z)] min = ℏ/(T • ∆M). The framework reveals mass spectrometry as intrinsically a state-counting process, with different analyzers representing different geometries for traversing partition space toward a common minimum. We propose the partition funnel as an optimal topology for ion transport based on direct partition descent with inherent damping from entropy generation during state transitions. Experimental validation using NIST glycan reference libraries achieves 100% conformance with the partition state space constraints, confirming the capacity formula C(n) = 2n 2 .

papers.title: Spherulites Certificate: A Dual-Layer Physical Authentication System Based on Humidity-Triggered Giant Spherulites in Lead-Halide Perovskite Hydrates
papers.abstract: We propose the Spherulites Certificate, a dual-layer physical authentication architecture that exploits the stochastic nucleation and macroscopic radial growth of lead-halide perovskite hydrate spherulites produced by Hygro-Triggered Giant Spherulites Formation (HT-GSF). Each thin-film label encodes two physically distinct information layers: a public layercomprising the geometric pattern of spherulite arms and the spatial coordinates of crystal nuclei-that is directly readable by an unmodified smartphone camera, and a private layer of sub-micrometre microstructural fingerprints accessible only by optical microscopy, retained exclusively by the issuing authority. A three-stage matching algorithm based on Delaunay triangulation of nucleus positions, histogram-of-oriented-gradients (HOG) texture descriptors, and probabilistic score fusion is proposed for public-layer verification. Collision probability analysis shows that for 10-20 nuclei on an 18 × 18 mm substrate at a spatial resolution of ±50 μm, the probability of two specimens sharing an identical nucleus configuration is in the range of 10 -52 to 10 -104 , far exceeding any practical uniqueness requirement. Comparison with established anti-counterfeiting technologies-including QR codes, holographic seals, NFC tags, and recently reported fluorescent and memristive perovskite PUF schemes-demonstrates structural advantages in clone resistance, readout accessibility, and security architecture. The Spherulites Certificate is positioned as a strong candidate for high-value authentication applications such as fine art provenance, pharmaceutical lot verification, and secure document issuance.

papers.title: Cancer as a Metabolic-Adaptive State Space: A Systems Framework Integrating Bioenergetics, Genome Maintenance, and Phenotypic Plasticity
papers.abstract: Cancer is often described by its mutations, tissue type, or molecular subtype, but these labels do not fully explain why tumours change over time, become resistant to treatment, or return after therapy. This paper explores a different way of thinking about cancer. Instead of treating cancer as one fixed condition, it models cancer as a changing adaptive system that can move between different biological states. In this framework, tumour cells are shaped not only by genetic alterations, but also by how they produce energy, which nutrients they depend on, how well they repair DNA damage, how they respond to stress, how healthy their mitochondria are, and how easily they can shift their identity. To study this idea, a simulation-based model was built using six biologically meaningful tumour states: Glycolytic Proliferative, OXPHOS Competent, Glutamine Addicted, Hybrid Plastic, Repair-Deficient Stressed, and Drug-Tolerant Adaptive. The model included features linked to glucose use, oxygenbased metabolism, glutamine dependence, lactate production, redox balance, DNA repair, replication stress, stem-like behavior, plasticity, proliferation, mitochondrial health, and drug tolerance. Different stress conditions, including nutrient shortage, low-oxygen-like stress, DNA-damaging stress, and therapy pressure, were then used to test how tumour cells might move from one state to another. The results showed that these simulated tumour states were clearly different from one another, but also biologically connected. Machine-learning analysis was able to distinguish the states with very high accuracy and strongly predict drug tolerance. The most important features shaping state identity were drug tolerance, stemness, glutamine uptake, plasticity, and GLS expression. Under therapy pressure, tumour cells tended to move toward a Drug-Tolerant Adaptive state, which was the most stable and hardest to escape. Overall, the study suggests that cancer may be better understood not as a static disease, but as movement through a structured adaptive landscape. This could help researchers identify weaknesses not only in tumour states themselves, but also in the routes cancer cells take to survive treatment.

papers.title: Freestanding Intrinsic Ferroelectric 2D Ice and Its 3D Stackings: Reshaping the Functional Boundaries of Low-Dimensional Hydrogen-Bonded Networks
papers.abstract: Can two-dimensional (2D) ice exist independently without a substrate? Can pure water serve as a functional material exhibiting ferroelectricity, semiconducting behavior, and extreme mechanical properties? These two fundamental questions have long remained unresolved. Here, through firstprinciples calculations, we provide the first theoretical confirmation that 2D ice can exist intrinsically and stably without any substrate. We discover a complete family of freestanding intrinsic ferroelectric 2D ice: parallelogram elemental 2D ice (P-Ice, stable at 5 K), biaxial ferroelectric origami-like topological 2D ice (O-Ice, stable at 260 K), and ferroelectric interlocked bilayer 2D ice (I-Ice, stable at 240 K). All three phases rigorously satisfy the golden criteria validation (entirely positive phonon spectra, Born-Huang mechanical stability criteria, and finitetemperature AIMD simulations). Notably, O-Ice and I-Ice maintain their structural integrity near the freezing point of water, providing the first demonstration that 2D hydrogen-bonded networks can survive independently without substrate support. Using these freestanding 2D ices as structural building blocks, we construct the first pure-water-based 3D ferroelectric materials via van der Waals stacking, achieving multilevel synergy between "in-plane hydrogen-bond ferroelectricity" and "interlayer van der Waals ferroelectricity." We uncover and validate a new principle: "2D order dictates 3D strength." These 3D stackings exhibit extraordinary mechanical properties-a Young's modulus along the Z-axis reaching 48.6 GPa (comparable to magnesium metal), a Poisson's ratio in the Y-X direction of 0.973 (approaching the theoretical limit), and a stiffness anisotropy of up to 6.5-fold. The layered frameworks remain structurally intact across a pressure range of 0-3000 GPa (spanning conditions from Earth's core to the interiors of ice giants), with an insulator-to-metal transition occurring at 1190 ± 20 GPa. This work resolves the long-standing debate over whether 2D ice must rely on substrates, elevating water from the most mundane substance to a functional material platform capable of independent existence. It opens new frontiers for green electronics, extreme-environment sensing, and planetary science.

papers.title: DeepHeal: Consensus Variational Autoencoder Atlases of Drug-Induced Proteomic Perturbations Enable Phenotype-Based Drug Discovery and Mechanism-of-Action Analysis
papers.abstract: Drug-perturbation proteomic profiles encode mechanism-relevant phenotypes, but robust latentspace models for large-scale perturbation proteomics remain underdeveloped. Here we developed DeepHeal, a framework comprising complementary consensus variational autoencoder atlases derived from 875 compound-induced proteomic log2FC profiles in HCT116, and used it for phenotype-based drug discovery, mechanism-of-action analysis and candidate prioritization. To our knowledge, this is the first application of variational autoencoders to large-scale drug-perturbation proteomics. Our primary atlas combined supervised contrastive learning with a 600-model consensus VAE ensemble so that the full cohort contributed to representation learning while 448 labelled compounds imposed class-aware structure; a matched unsupervised average-profile atlas served as reference. The supervised atlas retained 257 consensus latents and achieved perfect within-cohort separation of antineoplastic and nonantineoplastic compounds with both LGMLVQ and the best-performing AutoGluon classifier identified for the supervised branch (KNeighbors), whereas the average-profile atlas retained 194 latents and was weaker for classification (the best-performing AutoGluon classifier identified for the average-profile branch (TabM) accuracy 0.767, AUROC 0.756; LGMLVQ accuracy 0.767, AUROC 0.738). Pathway interpretation revealed a trade-off between density and breadth: the supervised atlas concentrated signal in cell-cycle, replicationstress and DNA-damage programmes and recovered 100 canonical pathways overall, whereas the averageprofile atlas preserved broader normalized pathway diversity per 100 latents in both canonical and oncogenic collections. Applying a stringent four-model consensus rule to 427 previously unlabelled compounds identified 19 high-confidence candidates, including 14 rediscovered external antineoplastics and a smaller set of mechanistically plausible repurposing candidates led by JP1302, BAY 61-3606 and SB 225002. Cluster-level and macro-mechanism analyses further resolved cohort-wide and subgroup-specific pathway structure across the atlas. These results establish DeepHeal as a practical framework for perturbation proteomics and show that proteomic latent atlases can support phenotypic screening, mechanism-of-action analysis and hypothesis generation within large drug-response resources.

papers.title: Steric-Induced Bending and Energy Level Shifts Induced by Covalently Bonding Anthracene to Si(111)
a-Aryl-a-Heteroarylmalononitriles via Proton-Transfer Dual-Ionization Nucleophilic Aromatic Substitution
papers.abstract: Herein we report the synthesis of a-aryl-a-heteroarylmalononitriles. Retrosynthetically, such molecules should be readily available from a-arylmalononitrile and haloheterocycles via nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr). Yet, these molecular-and reaction-classes are nearly unknown. Herein, it is described that traditional SNAr, basic conditions to yield nucleophilic a-arylmalononitrile anions, will not yield the target products. Rather, and simply, the products can arise under mild, formally neutral conditions by proton-transfer dual-ionization (PTDI) nucleophilic aromatic substitution (SNAr). This study includes a background analysis of aaryl-a-heteroarylmalononitriles and PTDI-SNAr, discovery and optimization of efficient coupling conditions, a study of various physical organic parameters governing the transformation, scope of the reaction, and applications in synthesis through malononitrile functional group interconversion.

papers.title: Cytotoxicity and Immunogenic Cell Death Studies of Water-soluble Tetrahedral Ga(III) or Fe(III) Coordination Cages Containing a Gold(I) Anticancer Drug as Guest
papers.abstract: The host-guest properties of Au(I) complexes encapsulated within water-soluble tetrahedral coordination cages of Ga(III) (1) or Fe(III) (2) were studied in solution and in cell cultures. FIN and FINester (FIN = triethylphosphine gold(I) complex of 4-mercaptobenzoate or ethyl ester) acted as guests in the coordination cages as shown by NMR spectroscopy and mass spectrometry studies. Ga(III)-FIN (1a) is stable in phosphate buffer solution for two days and in the presence of serum albumin for 24 h. Guests were encapsulated inside 1 or 2 at neutral or higher pH values but were released at the mildly acidic pH values (<6.5) characteristic of the extracellular tumor environment. The cytotoxicity response of the Ga(III) or Fe(III) cages with encapsulated FIN was assessed in two different cancer cell lines (human clear cell renal cell carcinoma ccRCC Caki-1 and murine colon carcinoma CT26) as well as normal cells (human fetal lung fibroblasts IMR-90) over a pH range of 7.5-6.2 and compared to the cages alone or gold drug alone. Whereas the cages alone were found to be moderately cytotoxic with some selectivity for cancer cells, FIN encapsulated in either Ga(III) or Fe(III) cages displayed a more selective cytotoxic response in cancer cell lines compared to normal cells. At mildly acidic pH, Fe-FIN-2a gave IC50 values of 4 µM in CT26 cells compared to 61 µM in IMR-90 cells. The free gold(I) complexes were the most highly cytotoxic but showed little selectivity for cancer cells compared to normal cells. Immunogenic cell death studies of FIN (with relevant anticancer properties) show that in Caki-1 it has significant release of DAMPs ATP and HGMB1 and elicits prominent CRT translocation at pH 7.2. In mildly acidic conditions (pH 6.5) there is a significant decrease in DAMPs release, and no translocation of CRT. Ga-FIN (2a) displays translocation of CRT under these conditions underscoring the potential of water-soluble cages to transport and stabilize gold drugs.

papers.title: An experiment-guided descriptor framework for chain-growth CO2 electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: The electroreduction of CO 2 to long-chain hydrocarbons (LCHC) has been recently demonstrated on several transition metal-based catalysts. However, the properties of the catalysts that open this pathway have yet to be fully elucidated. Here, we combine experiments and modeling to establish a set of descriptors across a series of transition-metal based catalysts, which will serve as a general framework in determining the efficacy of a catalyst for generating LCHC. We first experimentally show that strong *CO-binding catalysts such as Ni, Co, Fe, Ru, Rh, and Pd drive chain-growth CO 2 electrocatalysis toward LCHC. Hydrocarbon chain growth initiates from *CO formation and its hydrogenation to *CH x , followed by successive *CO insertion into a growing *RCH x chain. *CO hydrogenation and *CO-*CH x coupling are identified as the two key kinetic barriers governing chain growth. Guided by our experimental observations, density functional theory calculations were used to establish descriptors that rationalize LCHC formation. Unlike Cu (with moderate *CO binding) that favors *CO dimerization, strong *CO-binding catalysts favor *CO hydrogenation toward *CH x over *CO dimerization, thereby opening a route to LCHC. The relative barriers of *CO-*CH x coupling and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction further modulate LCHC yield. LCHC yield is further promoted by 3-7 fold across all catalysts by enhancing *CO hydrogenation under CO flow in a mildly acidic electrolyte. Overall, our results establish mechanistic descriptors and provide rational catalyst design principles for improving LCHC yield from CO 2 electroreduction.

papers.title: Bayesian Inference and Optimization for Design of Experiments in Chemical Kinetics
papers.abstract: Designing experimental campaigns to make efficient use of available time and resources is a critical task in any researchers day. For complex chemical engineering problems, model-based design of experiments (MBDOE) is a reliable tool to sequentially conduct optimal experiments. However, since this paradigm is built upon frequentist methods, uncertainty of data is oftentimes not considered in it despite being critical. On the other hand, Bayesian statistics methods allow for uncertainty modeling throughout the experimental design workflow. Here, a Bayesian design of experiments (bDOE) workflow is introduced leveraging Bayesian optimization (BO) in conjunction with three information-theory based acquisition functions to design optimal sequential experimental plans. It is demonstrated that the experimental budget can be reduced by approximately 60 % when parameterizing kinetic models using this methodology. Model discrimination can be achieved within very few (approximately four) specifically designed experiments. Overall, the proposed bDOE workflow lends itself to problems where the model structure is known but experiments are time-consuming, expensive or limited in number.

papers.title: Gateway to Data Visualization and Analysis in Solid-State Nanopores
authors: Y. M. Nuwan. D. Y. Bandara
papers.abstract: Solid-state nanopores are a class of single-molecule sensors with a growing footprint in molecular fingerprinting. Given the unique nature of experiments, data extraction, visualization, and interpretation are often carried out using customized software: an unacknowledged legacy barrier that stifles overall productivity and hinders entry for early-career researchers. With concerted efforts to democratize the solid-state nanopore technology and make it more accessible to a broader audience, there is a need to create a roadmap for data handling and processing associated with solid-state nanopores. In this work, we present a suite of apps and methods engineered to transition from raw ionic current traces to actionable data metrics. Our platform provides an integrated framework for the rigorous characterization of translocation events through the HyperXtract 2.0 app (HX2.0), which extracts over 50 distinct waveform features per event. To ensure data integrity, the quality of the nanopore is quantified using a suite of health parameters that underpin the biophysical reliability of the resulting waveforms. To facilitate multi-dimensional analysis, the software integrates specialized visualization modules for scatter plots, histograms, and non-linear curve fitting. It also includes high-density contour and heat maps (with clustering and denoising options), which are essential for resolving overlapping molecular populations that standard 1D plots might obscure. Collectively, bivariate contouring of waveform features from HX introduces a new path for the construction of QR-like molecular fingerprinting architecture. These apps considerably accelerate the data treatment step, empowering rapid and confident post-experiment decision-making.

papers.title: Recovery of Metals from Battery Materials with Electrogenerated Leaching Agents from CO2, O2 and H2O
papers.abstract: To recover the metals from lithium cobalt oxide (LCO) from batteries more sustainably, the application of electrochemically generated leaching agents from only CO2, O2 and H2O is presented. Therefore, CO2 was reduced to formic acid/formate and O2 was reduced to H2O2, each with high Faradaic efficiency (>85%) at gas diffusion electrodes. Formate and H2O2 were used individually or together to leach lithium and cobalt from LCO. When used together, mainly lithium was extracted while cobalt precipitated as insoluble cobalt phosphate, which allows efficient separation. Furthermore, lithium and cobalt could be leached almost quantitatively (Co: 99.6 ± 2.2%, Li: 92.7 ± 1.7%) by acidification with remarkably low amounts of sulfuric acid. In summary, this innovative feasibility study demonstrates that electrochemically generated leaching agents from air and water are a promising alternative to conventional leaching methods.

papers.title: Navigating high-dimensional spaces in chemistry and beyond with a reference-based coordinate assignment
papers.abstract: High-dimensional representations underpin modern machine learning across chemistry, biology, and data science, yet their rapidly increasing dimensionality limits scalability, interpretability, and computational e!ciency. Here we introduce the reference-based coordinate assignment (RCA), a geometric framework that reconstitutes dimensionality reduction as a positioning problem. Instead of deriving coordinates through global variance maximisation or optimisation-based projections, RCA determines positions from distances between investigated and reference samples, forming a new coordinate system. Using multilateration, data points are embedded relative to these references, enabling deterministic and pointwise embedding. Across diverse domains-including molecular datasets, image recognition, and speech classification-RCA produces compact representations that preserve the predictive power of machine learning models while dramatically reducing their computational cost. These results show that such reference distances can serve as scalable coordinates for complex data, providing an e!cient and interpretable framework for navigating high-dimensional spaces. How much, or how little information is necessary to represent a molecule to a machine to enable e!cient learning, su!ciently accurate property prediction, and accelerated discovery? Modern molecular representations encode structural and electronic information through hundreds or thou

papers.title: A Kinetic and Oxygen Poisoning Study of Ammonia Synthesis and Decomposition over the Supported MXene Mo2CTx
papers.abstract: The synthesis and decompositon of NH 3 have gained renewed attention in the context of using NH 3 as a renewable energy carrier. Both reactions require active catalysts based on earth-abundant metals that are also stable against common poisons. Here, we dispersed two-dimensional Mo 2 C T x MXene nanosheets onto SiO 2 to improve the accessibility of their active sites. In doing so, we achieved a ca. 10-fold improvement in Mo utilization for both reactions relative to an unsupported 3D β-Mo 2 Ν. A comparison with this reference catalyst showed that SiO 2 strongly affects the Mo active sites and alters the kinetic parameters of both reactions. For the NH 3 decomposition reaction, the support effect is stronger at lower Mo loadings, whereas at higher Mo loadings, a partial restacking occurs, and such Mo 2 C T x /SiO 2 catalysts behave similarly to bulk β-Mo 2 Ν. Interaction with the SiO 2 support increases the susceptibility of Mo 2 C T x to H 2 poisoning, but simultaneously enhances its stability to steam (at 8000 ppm). Additionally, SiO 2 limits the reducibility of Mo 2 C T x , thereby impeding the activation of N 2 and H 2 under NH 3 synthesis conditions. Unlike β-Mo 2 Ν, Mo 2 C T x /SiO 2 loses its activity at a CO 2 concentration of 210 ppm during NH 3 synthesis, explained by O* blocking of the active sites. CO 2 poisoning is only partially reversible due to the formation of inactive Mo 0 .

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence for Surfactant Science and Applications: A Review
papers.abstract: This paper reviews recent advances in applications of artificial intelligence methods to solve surfactants-related tasks. As variety of surfactant species and annual production are constantly growing, a new ways to characterize them are necessary. Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in the field of chemistry are promising instrument to perform such tasks. This review summarizes recent advances in the application of AI and machine learning (ML) to surfactant-related problems. After a brief overview of ML algorithms and typical workflows used in reviewed papers, the main applications of ML for quantitative structure-property relationship of intrinsic and industrial properties is discussed. Critical micelle concentration and surface tension are considered separately since they represent the most extensively studied properties. The review also discusses new rapidly evolving directions, including de novo generation of surfactant structures, duided experimental planning and developing of surfactant-based formulations. Finally, current challenges and future prospects of AI applications in surfactant science and applications are discussed. Overall, this review may provide solid foundation for future studies in the field and may become a good starting point for all interested researchers.

papers.title: Effect of Surface Heterogeneity on Electrolyte Stability in Mg-metal Batteries: Insights from Ab Initio Molecular Dynamics
authors: Sharma S R K C Yamijala
papers.abstract: Magnesium (Mg) metal batteries are widely regarded as a sustainable and high-capacity alternative to lithium-ion batteries. Despite their promise, their practical implementation is hindered by electrolyte instability at Mg metal anodes, which limits reversible Mg deposition and battery performance. In particular, widely-used Mg salts such as Mg(TFSI) 2 and Mg(PF 6 ) 2 have been the subject of conflicting experimental and computational reports, leaving the origins of electrolyte decomposition poorly understood. In this work, we address this critical knowledge gap by systematically examining interfacial stability of three representative salts, namely, Mg(TFSI) 2 , Mg(PF 6 ) 2 , and Mg(CB 11 H 12 ) 2 on three Mg anode surface models: metallic Mg (m-Mg), stoichiometric MgO (s-MgO), and non-stoichiometric MgO (ns-MgO), using ab initio molecular dynamics simulations. Our results demonstrate that oxide chemistry and surface heterogeneity critically dictate electrolyte stability. While m-Mg and s-MgO remain largely inert, ns-MgO surface triggers rapid anion decomposition, charge transfer, and irreversible passivation, explaining the experimental observations. Among the salts, Mg(CB 11 H 12 ) 2 shows exceptional stability across all surfaces, aligning with its reported cycling efficiency. Importantly, our study not only resolves the longstanding discrepancies between theory and experiment but also establishes a new computational framework that closely reflects experimental realities and provides critical atomistic insights into salt decomposition pathways.

papers.title: Quantifying the Number of Dark, Gray, and Bright States as a Function of Spectral Overlap in Polaritonic Systems
papers.abstract: Strong exciton-photon coupling can steer photophysical processes. However, the picture where the coupling leads to two polaritonic states and a manifold of optically dark states is now questioned. Instead, a picture where inhomogeneous broadening results in a partial photonic contribution to the dark states has gained ground. To understand the consequence of these dark and so-called gray states on polariton photophysics, they first need to be experimentally quantified. Here we use angle resolved emission, coupled to rate equation modelling to quantify the absolute number of dark states (approx. 10 6) in a series of optical cavities with different detunings. In addition, we also estimate the fraction of states that are gray by means of computer simulations. We find that the number of gray states is proportional to the overlap between the energy of the dark and polaritonic states. This knowledge can be applied readily to all previous and future studies to interpret how detuning affects the relative number of dark and gray states and, consequently, polaritonic dynamics.

papers.title: Skeletal Editing of Benzocyclobutenols toward Beonzo[b]furans
papers.abstract: An efficient 4-to-5 ring expansion through aryne intermediates is disclosed. A wide variety of iodo-substituted benzo[ b ]furans are prepared from benzocyclobutenols via unusual oxyiodonation of aryne intermediates. The great transformability of the resulting aryl iodides enables the access to diverse highly functionalized benzo[ b ]furans.

papers.title: Chiral Hafnium Phosphate Catalyzed Asymmetric De Mayo Reaction via Visible-Light-Induced Dearomatization
