papers.title: A reproducible molecular dynamics benchmark for ADC epitope triage in EGFR and HER2
papers.abstract: Antibody–drug conjugate programs often select epitopes before peptide-level mapping is available. Here I describe a reproducible molecular dynamics (MD) workflow for pre-HDX epitope triage in EGFR and HER2, evaluated on three therapeutic antibody–antigen pairs (EGFR–cetuximab, HER2–trastuzumab, EGFR–panitumumab). For each system, matched apo (antigen-only) and holo (Fab-bound) trajectories are reduced to residue-consistent antigen-only inputs and summarized into sliding peptide windows (W=12, stride=4) to generate a ranked list intended to guide first-pass HDX-MS peptide panel design. Primary directionality is fixed by a conservative protection proxy requiring both decreased exposure and decreased flexibility in holo relative to apo (BOTHNEG: ΔSASA(holo−apo)<0 and ΔRMSF(holo−apo)<0), with RMSF-only reported as a sensitivity check. To prevent off-interface stabilization from being misreported as epitope signal, ranked windows are constrained using geometric proximity to the antibody interface defined from available complex structures, and interface residues are summarized as an evidence-weighted core and an extended interface-supported set. Robustness is assessed using matched-interval truncation checks (EGFR–cetuximab Rep2; HER2–trastuzumab Rep2) and a matched time-split analysis for panitumumab (0–15 vs 15–30 ns) to make time sensitivity explicit. For EGFR–cetuximab and HER2–trastuzumab, ranked interface-localized regions are compared to published protection patterns and structural interface loop mapping. For EGFR–panitumumab, peptide-level HDX-MS labels are not used; evaluation is performed against proxy anchors derived from crystallographic contacts and mutational footprint evidence on EGFR domain III. This work is positioned as a pre-HDX triage and benchmarking layer that generates auditable, testable peptide-panel hypotheses rather than predicting absolute deuterium uptake kinetics or clinical efficacy.

papers.title: Quantifying photochemical propulsion in light-powered Janus micromotors
papers.abstract: Active colloids that convert light into motion provide insight into non-equilibrium chemical systems and routes toward microscale engines. Here we quantify the propulsion dynamics and force generation of light-activated Au-TiO 2 Janus particles and their optically trappable polystyrene (PS) core-shell Au-PS@TiO 2 analogues. By varying particle size, metal thickness, fuel concentration, and illumination wavelength, we show how photochemical energy conversion at the Au-TiO 2 interface governs propulsion, yielding average velocities 33.2 ± 2.99 μm s⁻¹ with instantaneous velocities up to ~100 μm s⁻¹. Optical tweezers measurements on single Au-PS@TiO 2 Janus particles reveal transient propulsion forces with a median of 4.5-6.2 pN lasting on average 21-41 ms and reaching up to 20 pN. Simulations incorporating these transient forces reproduce the observed trajectories, confirming their role in driving active motion. Functionalization with long DNA polymers further enhances directional motion by reducing rotational diffusion. These results establish a single-particle framework for quantifying active forces in photocatalytic Janus particles and offer design principles for light-powered micromotors.

papers.title: Exploring Performance Tradeoffs in Redox-mediated Flow Batteries
papers.abstract: Redox-mediated flow batteries (RMFBs), an emerging subclass of redox flow batteries (RFBs), incorporate solid active materials into the tanks to dramatically increase theoretical energy density, albeit currently at the expense of design and operational simplicity. Using physics-based models, we assess the performance tradeoffs inherent to these systems, with an emphasis on understanding what factors most impact accessible power and energy densities and how this new concept compares to conventional RFBs. Through sensitivity analyses and sampling methods, we identify key dimensionless parameters with the greatest influence on system capacity (e.g., Damköhler numbers and dimensionless current) and reveal a “collapsed relationship” that effectively captures the predicted solid utilization. We assess the distinct tradeoffs in cell power, pumping losses, and solid utilization associated with RMFBs, by tuning physical and operating parameters (e.g., particle size and current). Ultimately, we identify favorable property profiles that enable desirable power and energy characteristics. Finally, we reflect on the implications of these analyses, translating the model-based findings into engineering guidance and intuition on the relative merits of single- versus dual-mediator systems, on the general importance of mediator concentration for power density, and on design strategies to balance electrochemical and fluid dynamic performance.

papers.title: From Sequence to Redox-Responsive Assembly: Coarse-Grained Simulation, Network Analysis, and Interpretable Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Stimuli-responsive self-assembly, in which a chemical trigger reversibly switches peptide aggregation state, holds broad promise for smart materials and drug delivery, yet its sequence-level determinants remain largely unexplored by simulation. We report a large-scale computational screening of 28,557 di-, tri-, and tetrapeptide sequences for redox-responsive self-assembly using paired coarse-grained molecular dynamics (MARTINI 2.2) in free monomeric and disulfide-linked dimeric forms. We introduce dEdge, the change in intermolecular contact count upon dimerization, as a direct, SASA-independent metric that resolves redox-responsive behavior more reliably than conventional aggregation propensity scores. Network-based topology classification establishes that these short peptides occupy a structural space outside all canonical amyloid fibril classes. Network Hamiltonian Model (NHM) parameterization characterizes this space thermodynamically, revealing that the monomer-to-dimer transition involves a multi-dimensional shift from transient, loosely connected networks to geometrically clustered, cohesive assemblies, with sequence-specific fingerprints that identify the most structurally responsive candidates. A Transformer encoder predicts dEdge from sequence alone with high accuracy (MAE=0.146, RMSE=0.184), and Integrated Gradients analysis extracts actionable design rules: polar and acidic residues at the N-terminus strongly promote dimer-favoring assembly while aromatic residues suppress it, a pattern corroborated by direct mutation analysis. The simulation dataset, NHM parameter library, and interpretable predictive model constitute a sequence-to-function resource for designing redox-responsive self-assembling peptide materials.

papers.title: Nonequilibrium ab initio modeling of electrocatalysis
papers.abstract: We present a nonequilibrium ab initio approach for modeling electrocatalysis using steady-state density functional theory (SS-DFT), where nonequilibrium effects are incorporated through Hershfield quantum statistics. In the equilibrium limit, where the working electrode potential U equals the potential of zero charge U PZC , our SS-DFT approach reduces to the constant-charge DFT (DFT-CC). When | U - U PZC | is small, the linear response approximation (LRA) simplifies the SS-DFT effective energy to a quadratic form on electrode potential U . Although analogous to the constant-potential DFT (DFT-CP) formulation, the resulting expression contains a distinct prefactor that incorporates nonequilibrium effects. Using N 2 adsorption on an Au(310) cathode as an example, our calculations for adsorption free energies show that the SS-DFT approach accurately reproduces the DFT-CC results at U = U PZC , exhibits quadratic -dependence in excellent agreement with the LRA for | U - U PZC | < 0.5 V , and predicts significant nonequilibrium effects for | U - U PZC | > 0.5 V . Further calculations for electrochemical N 2 reduction reaction (NRR) reveal that potential-dependent nonequilibrium effects, which are not captured in standard DFT approaches, are essential for explaining the experimentally reported high electrocatalytic activity of Au(310) for NRR.

papers.title: From Spectra to Local Networks: Evaluating MS² Similarity Metrics
papers.abstract: MS² spectral similarity is fundamental to interpreting LC-HRMS-NTA data. Beyond the commonly used cosine similarity, a wide range of alternative metrics, including distance-, probability-, and machine-learning–based approaches, provide different perspectives on spectral matching. In this study, we extracted 8,290 subdatasets from publicly available LC-HRMS/MS libraries (MassBank, MoNa, GNPS, and NIST), each containing spectra sharing a precursor m/z within a 5 mDa tolerance. We evaluated 20 similarity metrics by constructing single-generation local molecular networks. Most metrics failed to produce pure networks, achieving complete resolution in only ~8% of cases at the recommended 0.7 threshold and ~20% even when individually optimized. The number of fragment ions showed little influence on network resolution. Instead, performance was driven primarily by the similarity metric and thresholding behavior, indicating that library matching alone rarely supports identification confidence above level 3. These findings highlight the need for cumulative strategies that integrate multiple similarity perspectives and orthogonal information, such as retention time or index.

papers.title: Perturbation of Nanoplastics on Biomembranes: Molecular Insights from Neutron Scattering
papers.abstract: Plastic waste is now pervasive in the environment, breaking down into microplastics and nanoplastics under many environmental conditions. These particles have been found in various ecosystems and even in human tissues, raising significant environmental and health concerns. In this study, we investigated the interaction of polystyrene nanoplastics, with and without surface modifications, on biomembrane structures using contrast-matching small-angle neutron scattering and neutron spin echo spectroscopy. The neutron contrast matching enabled selective study of biomembranes in the presence of nanoplastics. Two model membranes were employed: a simple zwitterionic bilayer (i.e., dimyristoylphosphatidylcholine [DMPC]) and an Escherichia coli lipid extract as a bacterial membrane model. The results show profound membrane disruptions, including possible thinning, vesicle fragmentation, lipid monolayer formation, and inter-vesicle aggregation, with the more severe effects observed in DMPC membranes. Notably, E. coli membranes exhibited greater resilience, suggesting that natural membranes with diverse lipid compositions may reduce susceptibility to perturbation by extracellular nanoplastics. These findings highlight potential risks posed by environmental nanoplastic particles to biological membranes, with insights into molecular-level interactions and the environmental toxicity of nanoplastics. This work provides a foundation for future studies into nanoplastic–biomembrane interactions and their broader implications for health and environment using neutrons.

papers.title: Fluoride-Excess Synthesis of CaF₂ Nano-powder: Tuning Conductivity for Fluoride Ion Batteries (FIB)
papers.abstract: Calcium fluoride (CaF₂) nano-powders were prepared by a polyol-mediated synthesis under fluoride-excess conditions. By varying the initial fluorine precursor concentration, we induced fluoride anti-Frenkel defects (fluoride-ion interstitials with corresponding vacancies) and increased the concentration of fluoride-diethylene glycol (DEG) complexes at the nanoparticle surface. Precursors were mixed at Ca:F ratios of 0.50, 0.40, and 0.35 (denoted samples DE8, DE9, and DE10, respectively) to study the effect of stoichiometry on the final CaF₂ nano-powders. The structure, morphology, and ionic conductivity of these materials were examined. X-ray diffraction (XRD) confirmed that the CaF₂ nano-powders crystallize in the fluorite-type face-centered cubic (FCC) structure (space group Fm-3m) with an average core crystallite size of ~8 nm, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) showed particle sizes around 14-18 nm. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) analyses revealed the presence of fluorideexcess defect structures in the material. The best-performing composition (Ca:F = 0.35) exhibited an improved ionic conductivity of approximately 2×10 −5 S•cm −1 at 40 °C. This solid electrolyte was successfully implemented in a fluoride ion battery (FIB) test cell using a magnesium anode and a BiF₃ cathode, demonstrating room-temperature battery operation.

papers.title: Synchronous rotation dynamics in a molecular motor
papers.abstract: Direct measurements of molecular motion during chemical reactions are essential to understand how molecular machines perform work. In most systems, however, the reaction rate is dictated by the probability of reaching the transition state, thereby masking the underlying molecular motions. Here, we study the dynamics of rotation around the central double bond of an artificial light-driven molecular motor by femtosecond transient absorption and fluorescence spectroscopy. We observe a first rotation step of 28° which occurs synchronously across the motor ensemble and without an activation barrier, such that the measurements are representative of molecular dynamics. We can thus estimate the rotation speed and the relative importance of inertia, friction and strain, and propose a simplified nanomechanical model for the molecular motor. The results promise a new window of investigation into work at the nanoscale, and provide tools to analyze the mechanics of molecular machines, both synthetic or biological.

papers.title: Electronic tongue detection of adulteration in ginseng-based erectile dysfunction supplements
papers.abstract: Liquid chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry remains the gold standard for the analysis of pharmaceuticals and dietary supplements. However, due to high costs and long analysis times, this technique is not suitable for large-scale screening. Although dietary supplements are legally classified as food products, they are often manufactured in pharmaceutical dosage forms and are not subject to mandatory quality control, which makes them particularly susceptible to adulteration. Therefore, there is an ongoing need for rapid, cost-effective, and easily accessible analytical techniques capable of screening dietary supplements available on the market. In this work, an electronic tongue system was proposed to detect adulteration with sildenafil (a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor) in one of the most frequently adulterated dietary supplement categories. Five ginseng-based dietary supplements for erectile dysfunction and their counterparts artificially adulterated with sildenafil were investigated employing an array of cross-sensitive potentiometric sensors. Recorded sensor responses were subjected to multivariate data analysis, including PCA and PLS-DA. The multisensor system successfully discriminated between authentic and artificially adulterated samples. Moreover, undeclared sildenafil was detected in one of the tested products and subsequently confirmed by UHPLC-MS. These results demonstrate that the electronic tongue is a suitable screening method for detecting adulteration in ginseng-based dietary supplements.

papers.title: Analytical Method Development in Pharmaceutical Sciences: A Comprehensive Review of Contemporary Frameworks, Lifecycle Approaches, and Regulatory Considerations
papers.abstract: Analytical method development constitutes a foundational pillar of pharmaceutical quality assurance, underpinning the generation of reliable data for drug substance and drug product characterization, release testing, and stability evaluation. This review examines the current state of analytical method development within the pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and medical device industries, with particular emphasis on the evolving regulatory landscape shaped by the International Council for Harmonisation (ICH) guidelines Q2(R2) and Q14. The article explores the traditional one-factor-at-a-time (OFAT) approach to method development and contrasts it with the enhanced, systematic methodology promoted under the Analytical Quality by Design (AQbD) framework. Key elements of the enhanced approach are discussed, including the Analytical Target Profile (ATP), risk assessment strategies, design of experiments (DoE), and the establishment of a Method Operable Design Region (MODR). The lifecycle management concept, encompassing method design, performance qualification, and continued performance verification, is explored as a unifying paradigm that connects development activities to routine use and post-approval changes. Challenges to widespread AQbD adoption, including resource constraints, knowledge gaps, and the absence of mandated regulatory requirements, are critically evaluated. The article concludes by examining future directions, including the integration of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and process analytical technology into method development workflows, and offers practical recommendations for organizations seeking to transition from traditional to enhanced development strategies.

papers.title: Hydrophobic Ion Pairing Improves Protein Thermal Stability and Lipid Nanocarrier Integration Through Controlled Surface Modification
papers.abstract: Integrating therapeutic proteins into lipid-based nanocarriers remains challenging due to fundamental incompatibilities between hydrophilic protein surfaces and lipophilic carrier matrices. Here, we demonstrate that controlled hydrophobic ion pairing (HIP) using lysozymesodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) at stoichiometric ratios simultaneously improves thermal stability during pharmaceutical processing and lipid compatibility for nanocarrier integration. Building on our previous molecular characterisation of lysozyme-SDS complexes, we investigated their application in nanostructured lipid carriers (NLC) formulations for oral protein delivery. SDS complexation preserved lysozyme enzymatic activity at processing-relevant temperatures and increased apparent lipid miscibility by 50% in both solid and liquid pharmaceutical lipid excipients. This enhanced compatibility translated directly into superior NLC performance, with complexed lysozyme achieving a 4-fold higher encapsulation efficiency (79.6 ± 1.8% vs. 18.4 ± 4.3% for native protein) with improved batch-to-batch reproducibility. In simulated gastrointestinal conditions, lysozyme-SDS NLCs demonstrated sustained intestinal release (87.2 ± 16.5% over 6 hours) with 67.5 ± 7.5% enzymatic activity retained compared to only 15.2 ± 3.0% activity for native lysozyme formulations. Mechanistic analysis from differential scanning calorimetry and crystallinity measurements showed that SDS complexation induces a molten globule-like protein state that reduces lipid packing (56.8% vs. 68.6% crystallinity for native lysozyme), enabling superior matrix integration while maintaining biological function. These findings establish that controlled surface modification through HIP provides a systematic approach to overcome protein-lipid incompatibilities, offering a generalizable framework for developing lipid-based protein therapeutics.

papers.title: Skeletal Remodelling of Bicyclo[1.1.0]butanes to All-Carbon Quaternary Oxindoles
papers.abstract: Scaffold remodelling, involving controlled deconstruction and reconstruction, streamlines chemical synthesis and offers efficient retrosynthetic strategies. However, the remodelling of bicyclo[1.1.0]butane (BCB), a valuable synthetic building block, remains underexplored and has largely been limited to the formation of cyclopropanes. Herein, we report a palladium-catalyzed remodelling of BCB that proceeds through sequential deconstruction and reconstruction to deliver functionalized all-carbon quaternary oxindoles. The reaction accommodates diverse substituents on both aryl halides and BCBs. A subsequent cascade transforms the initial oxindole into a triarylated product via a Heck reaction, forming four CC bonds in a single operation. Furthermore, the obtained compounds serve as valuable precursors to spiroindoline derivatives. The isolation of key intermediates along with mechanistic experiments supports the proposed mechanistic pathway.

papers.title: Rapid and Facile Spectrophotometric Method for the Selective Determination of Peroxymonosulfate, Peroxydisulfate and Hydrogen Peroxide in Ternary Mixtures
papers.abstract: Peroxides such as peroxydisulfate (PDS), peroxymonosulfate (PMS) and hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) are important bulk oxidants used in wastewater treatment, bleaching or leaching. In many of these processes and during electrosynthesis, they often coexist in complex mixtures. Selective quantification of each peroxide constitutes a fundamental step towards understanding and optimizing these processes. However, achieving selectivity poses a major analytical challenge since most quantification methods rely on the oxidative properties towards indicators and interference through coexisting peroxides is common. In this study, the different iodide oxidation kinetics of PDS, PMS, and H 2 O 2 were utilized to differentiate between them. Time-resolved spectrophotometry at 350 nm under optimized assay conditions was established as a prerequisite for achieving sufficient selectivity and reliable quantification. Employing low iodide concentrations and short reaction times, enable selective PMS quantification. By adding molybdate catalyst, the determination of H 2 O 2 is realized. Finally, the PDS concentration is derived from the total peroxide content obtained under optimized assay conditions by subtracting the H 2 O 2 and PMS concentration. The assay sensitivities reach 7.62 × 10 3 M −1 (PMS), 7.68 × 10 3 M −1 (H 2 O 2 ) and 4.1 × 10 3 M −1 (PDS) while the limit of quantification is as low as 6.6 µM (PMS), 3.9 µM (H 2 O 2 ) and 17 µM (PDS). The degree of interference caused by coexisting peroxides was thorougly investigated and the proposed quantification procedure was successfully applied to real electrolysis samples. The simplicity and reliability of the developed method enables high-throughput screening of electrodes, electrolytes or reaction conditions and allows quality control of processes.

papers.title: Quinones and tyrosines in the long-range donor-acceptor side interactions in photosystem II: Implications for proton-coupled electron transfer
papers.abstract: It has long been known that certain changes in the acceptor (reductive) side of the Photosystem II (PSII) reaction center lead to alterations on the donor (oxidative) side. However, the nature of this long-range interaction remains unclear. In PSII, the proton-coupled electron transfer is carried out by plastoquinones, Q A and Q B , on the acceptor side and by the tyrosine residues, D1-Tyr161 (Tyr Z ) and D2-Tyr160 (Tyr D ), on the donor side. All four redox components share a similar head-group structure, are symmetrically located on the D1 and D2 core proteins and interact with histidine residues that serve as H-bonding partners. These histidine residues are D1-His215 (His B ), D1-His190 (His Z ), D2-His214 (His A ) and D2-His189 (His D ) respectively. The corresponding histidines of the Q B /Tyr Z pair and Q A /Tyr D pair are bound by the same transmembrane α-helix D of the corresponding D1 or D2 protein ~35 Å apart. It is hypothesized that changes in H-bonding accompanying reduction of acceptor side components are propagated along α-helix D, inducing corresponding alterations in the H-bonding of the donor side components, thereby facilitating their oxidation, and vice versa. Thus, the specific H-bond environment of the single electron acceptor Q A determines the oxidized state of Tyr D in active PSII. When Tyr D is oxidized, Q A is more favorably poised to accept an electron and to transfer it to Q B . On the other hand, the proton-coupled electron reduction and exchange of Q B governs Tyr Z oxidation and reduction during PSII turnover. The structural, functional and evolutionary implications of the proposed mechanism of long-range interactions in PSII are discussed in the context of possible computational and experimental methodologies that can be employed to test this hypothesis.

papers.title: Prebiotic-type small molecules preferentially bind ancient protein architectures
papers.abstract: Proteins inferred to trace back to the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) represent deeply conserved biological architectures that emerged within a chemically simpler environment than that produced by contemporary metabolism. Here, prebiotic-type small molecules from ChemOrigins were integrated with high-confidence binding data from ChEMBL and protein targets were classified by evolutionary conservation using orthologous group analysis. Binding patterns of prebiotic compounds were compared to clinically investigated molecules across stringent (≤1 µM) and relaxed (≤100 µM) activity thresholds, with additional controls for shared target space and physicochemical matching. Prebiotic compounds exhibited significant enrichment for LUCA-level protein targets relative to clinical compounds at both activity cutoffs (odds ratio up to 6.26 at ≤1 µM, p = 6.1 × 10⁻⁵), with enrichment persisting under multiple analytical constraints. Physicochemical matching confirmed that the effect is not solely due to differences in size, polarity, or structural complexity. LUCA-binding compounds occupied an intermediate region of chemical space between prebiotic molecules and modern non-LUCA-binding compounds, and local structural similarity to prebiotic chemistry was enriched among LUCA binders, particularly at higher similarity thresholds. Together, these findings suggest that evolutionarily ancient protein architectures retain preferential compatibility with small molecules from prebiotic chemical space. This enrichment motivates experimental tests in which prebiotic-inspired fragment libraries are screened against panels of LUCA-level and evolutionarily younger proteins to directly assess preferential chemical compatibility across evolutionary depth. More broadly, incorporating prebiotic plausibility as a library design axis may offer a complementary strategy for drug discovery targeting deeply conserved proteins.

papers.title: Nonpolar Resonance Controls Polar Cycloadditions through Transient Electromeric Charge Redistribution
papers.abstract: The electronic influence of substituents on chemical reactivity has long been described in terms of mesomeric and electromeric effects—concepts introduced nearly a century ago and now broadly unified under the IUPAC term “resonance effect”, which no longer considers them as independent. In 2002, however, the electromeric effect—transient electron redistribution in the presence of the second reaction center—was reinvented by Liu et al. under the name of “nonpolar resonance effect” to explain thermodynamics of nonpolar reactions exhibiting non-Hammett behavior. They noted that low polarity is a prerequisite for its observation. Here, we combine experiments and computations to demonstrate that electromeric effect—we adopt its historic name—controls the closure of zwitterionic intermediate in a reaction between pyridinium ylides and nitroalkenes: it stabilizes the transition state, making the reaction feasible for polarizable substituents in spite of their donor or acceptor nature. Our results imply that polarizable substituents can stabilize transition states even when their electron demands counteract the usual electronic preferences of substituents. We propose that similar electronic and reactivity patterns might be observed in other transformations, suggesting that the recently revived electromeric effect is more widespread than previously recognized.

papers.title: A reaction-aware autonomous platform co-optimizing formulation and execution for the synthesis of zeolitic imidazolate framework
papers.abstract: Autonomous experimentation is transforming materials discovery, yet most platforms rely on endof-run measurements, ignoring reaction-progress information and imposing rigid execution protocols. Here, we present Axo, a reaction-aware batch autonomous platform that integrates timeresolved in situ optical monitoring into liquid-handling synthesis. Each run is recorded as a reaction trajectory and converted into two kinetic descriptors: the extent of reaction that adapts measurement interval and batch size to match the reaction timescale, and the nucleation rate constant (𝑘 𝑛 ) that guides the Bayesian optimization of formulation variables. Applied to the solution-phase crystallization of zeolitic imidazolate framework-67 (ZIF-67 , Axo identified a rapid-nucleation region with 𝑘 𝑛 = 2.33 min -1 , exceeding the best condition found by static maximin sampling by over five-fold. This work demonstrates how programmable in situ trajectories can be converted into actionable feedback that enables reaction-aware closed-loop optimization to cooptimize what to test and how to measure in solution-phase materials synthesis.

papers.title: Reactivity of CO 2 with isopropanol in gas phase under mild temperature conditions using Ni/CeO 2 catalysts
Engineering Antifreeze Proteins to Optimally Resist Engulfment by Ice
papers.abstract: Antifreeze proteins (AFPs) facilitate the survival of organisms in cold climates by inhibiting the growth and/or recrystallization of ice. To function, AFPs must first bind to ice crystals; bound AFPs must then resist engulfment by using their nonbinding side (NBS) to pin the ice-water interface. Here we seek to understand how the molecular characteristics of an NBS, such as its ice-phobicity or shape, influence its ability to resist engulfment. By characterizing the free energy barriers that impede the engulfment of model AFPs, we find that the critical supercooling ∆T* , above which an AFP is engulfed, is dictated by an optimal pinning site on the NBS. We further find that the optimal pinning site is determined by an interplay between the contact line perimeter P and a pinning efficiency η, with ∆T* ∝ ηP at the optimal pinning site. For a hemispherical AFP, which displays progressively inward tapering, we find that η increases during engulfment, whereas P decreases; conversely, an NBS with outward tapering can achieve high P , but suffers from low η. Because the product of η and P determines ∆T* , the inverse correlation between them limits ∆T*. To circumvent such limiting behavior, we propose an NBS shape with an outward bulge; by initially tapering outwards, a bulged NBS permits higher P , and by subsequently tapering inwards, it promotes high η as well. Importantly, we find that ∆T* is enhanced by more than a factor of two with an outward bulge of only 1 nm. We also find that the more ice-phobic an NBS is, the more efficiently it pins the ice-water interface, resulting in higher ∆T*. Our findings thus shed light on how the NBS molecular characteristics influence ∆T* , and suggest strategies for engineering the NBS to optimally resist engulfment by ice.

papers.title: Chitosan-GSNO Nanogel Interacting with a Tomato Cuticle Biomimetic Membrane: A Multiscale Spectroscopy-Simulation Study
papers.abstract: Delivering nitric oxide (NO) in a controlled and barrier-preserving manner is essential for dermocosmetic, agricultural, and pharmaceutical applications. Using coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations combined with nanoscale vibrational spectroscopy, we show that a chitosan-TPP-GSNO nanoparticle provides a stable reservoir of NO that interacts selectively with the interfacial region of a-carotene-enriched cuticular membrane. The nanoparticle remains fully solvated and non-adsorbing, avoiding membrane disruption while subtly modulating lipid fluidity. NO remains confined to the headgroup region, where it can react efficiently without penetrating or destabilizing the barrier. Experimental Raman measurements on plant cuticles validate the predicted interfacial reactivity and structural preservation. These results establish a non-invasive, tunable NO-delivery mechanism with strong potential for enhancing skin treatment efficacy, improving postharvest fruit preservation, and enabling localized therapeutic release in lipid-rich biological interfaces.

papers.title: Fusing Delta Learning and Machine Learned Interatomic Potentials for Efficient High Throughput Calculation of Surface Kinetic Parameters
papers.abstract: Heterogeneous catalysis is critical in most industrial chemical processes. Microkinetic models can be used to greatly facilitate optimization of catalyst design and process conditions, but require thermochemical and kinetic parameters for all relevant species 1 and reactions. Our software Pynta enables fully automated calculation of thermochemical and kinetic parameters, however, the computational cost of density functional theory (DFT) calculations makes it difficult to calculate kinetic parameters at scale. In this work, we combine finetuning of the MACE multi-head v0 model with graph-based delta learning of stationary points using subgraph isomorphic decision trees (SIDT). We first generate a target chemical space on Pt111 by using the Reaction Mechanism Generator (RMG) software to generate all possible surface reactions between a set of 153 chemically adsorbed species containing C,H,N, and O. Applying Pynta to this reaction set we are able to generate geometries for many gas phase species, adsorbates and transition states in this chemical space allowing us to efficiently sample near stationary points for finetuning and stationary points for delta learning. In particular, we adapt Pynta's harmonically force saddle point search (HFSP) algorithm to enable efficient and reliable sampling of near transition state points. With this training data we show that SIDT-driven delta learning of the foundation MLIP alone can achieve similar accuracies on enthalpies to foundation model finetuning approaches. However, we show that by combining the two approaches into one framework we are able to significantly improve our accuracies over either approach allowing us to achieve 0.07 eV MAE relative to DFT on test barrier heights. Applying this framework across all reactions in our chemical space, we are able to obtain near DFT accuracy rate coefficients for 3111 reactions on Pt(111).

papers.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Antibody-mediated Effector Function Using Structural Features of Fc-Glycans and Binding Affinity to an Fc-receptor
papers.abstract: Fc-glycosylation critically modulates antibody effector functions including antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) and antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP), yet computational tools for predicting Fc-receptor binding affinity remain limited. Here, we present a systematic machine learning benchmark evaluating 10 machine learning methods for predicting Fc binding affinity to FcγRIIIa receptor which is responsible for the ADCC activity. Using a curated dataset of 22 structurally diverse N-glycans on antibodies with experimentally measured binding affinities of antibody-glycoforms FcγRIIIa-receptor, we compared traditional machine learning approaches using glycan structural motif features against deep learning methods employing pretrained graph neural network embeddings. Support vector regression with a linear kernel achieved the best performance (Spearman ρ = 0.85), followed closely by ElasticNet (ρ = 0.82) and Ridge regression (ρ = 0.81). Notably, simpler linear models consistently outperformed more complex ensemble methods and deep learning approaches, with the pretrained SweetNet graph neural network yielding substantially lower correlation (ρ = 0.58). The superior performance of linear models suggests that glycan structural motifs capture essential features to predict receptor binding affinity. Our rigorous nested leave-one-out cross-validation protocol with bootstrap confidence intervals provides robust performance estimates suitable for small datasets. This study demonstrated that by decoding the impact of Fc-glycosylation on Fc-receptor binding, we can build the dataset for AI-driven prediction of ADCC, and this approach is extensible to other Fc receptors and the corresponding effector functions

papers.title: A General Approach to Tryptophan-Crosslinked Macrocyclic Peptides Enabled by a Dual Functional Directing Group
papers.abstract: Tryptophan-crosslinked macrocyclic peptides have recently emerged as an exciting class of natural products with intricate structures and therapeutic properties 1-4. While their biosynthesis and biological functions have been explored 2,5-8 , simple and broadly applicable chemical methods for their total synthesis are not available. Here we report a general approach toward the synthesis of these rigid and complex peptides using rhodium-catalyzed intramolecular transannular macrocyclization. The success and broad applicability of the approach relies on a mechanistically-guided design and detailed computational analyses of the catalytic cycle, to arrive at a dual-function nucleophilic pyridyl directing group, which enables orthometalation and nucleophilic carbon-nitrogen bond formation in complex molecular settings. We demonstrate the utility of this method by synthesizing, among others, the pharmacophore s of micitide-982 and the potent antibiotic tryglysin.

papers.title: Dual-SplitNluc: A Spectrally Resolved Bioluminescence Platform Enabling Duplex Homogeneous Immunoassays
papers.abstract: Bioluminescence (BL)-based assays are broadly used for genetic reporter assays, imaging, as well as in vitro biomarker or serological analysis. However, nearly all existing BL assays are operated in a single-channel mode, which limits the detection capacity to one analyte each time. To extend the potential of BL assays, we developed the Dual-SplitNluc platform, a spectrally resolved BL reporter system which enables simultaneous detection of two analytes in homogeneous format based on spectral unmixing. Dual-SplitNluc represents the integration of our previously reported SplitNluc system together with SplitNanoBRET, an orange-emitting complementation-based immunoassay platform derived from SplitNluc. With chemical modification of the SplitNluc reporter by adding a fluorophore acting as a BL resonance energy transfer (BRET) acceptor, red-shifted photon emission can be generated and spectrally separated from the conventional SplitNluc signal. Through mathematical deconvolution of the integrated luminescence readouts, the original BL signals from each individual analyte can be extracted and utilized for ratiometric or quantitative analysis of both analytes. Collectively, Dual-SplitNluc extends BL assays beyond the single-analyte mode and provides a generalizable strategy for duplex and potentially higher-order multiplex homogeneous detection using spectral resolution as an orthogonal analytical dimension.

papers.title: Using weighted and chopped rectangular collocation methods with tensor-product contracted bases to compute vibrational spectra: avoiding quadrature
papers.abstract: Product contracted (PC) bases are efficient for computing (ro-)vibrational spectra of molecules. However, to account for coupling between subsystems all previous PC methods require computing integrals by quadrature. The cost of the quadrature is significant and increases with the dimensionality of the molecule. In this paper, we propose a weighted and chopped rectangular collocation (WC-RC) method that obviates quadrature. We use Christoffel weights and Christoffel-Fekete (CF) collocation points. They are known to be near-optimal for weighted least squares fitting. Matrix chopping increases the accuracy of energy levels. An additional chopping makes it possible to symmetry-adapted (SA) the calculation. With the WC-RC method, we achieve sub-0.1 cm −1 accuracy for both 9-D CH 2 NH and 6-D HF dimer, using many fewer points than required when quadrature is used.

papers.title: Selective Covalent Assembly of Gram-negative Bacteria and Synthetic Polymers into Functional Living Materials
papers.abstract: Here, we report selective covalent assembly of gram-negative bacteria and synthetic polymers into functional living materials. We discovered that telechelic polymers decorated with vinyl sulfone (VS), a motif that forms a stable covalent bond with cysteine residues on surface proteins, yielded stable covalent assembly with bacterial cells. Notably, we found that these assemblies were uniquely cell-type-specific, occurring only in Gram-negative bacteria, highlighting differences in surface structures and the macromolecular diffusion barrier across bacterial species. We also demonstrated that assembling engineered cells into materials results in situ melanin production from living materials, with robust biocontainment and mechanical reinforcement. Spontaneous enrichment of tyrosine-derived red pigments in the supernatant showcases the effect of confinement in a complex biochemical pathway. This work establishes a platform for encoding complex, engineered, and evolved functions of gram-negative bacteria into synthetic materials, enabling the development of a wide range of material-based bioreactors.

papers.title: PROx-Tag: p-phenylenediamine warheads enable photosensitized proximity labeling with high sensitivity and spatial resolution
papers.abstract: Photoproximity labeling (PPL) has emerged as an attractive alternative to enzymatic approaches for probing protein interactomes owing to its potentially greater spatiotemporal control, resolution and biocompatibility. However, applications inside living cells with conventional high-energy photocatalysts remain limited. Efforts to employ a broader array of genetically targetable photosensitizers for facile intracellular PPL have largely relied on singlet oxygen-mediated histidine oxidation, necessitating high doses (0.25-20 mM) of the proximity labeling reagent to outcompete water and endogenous nucleophiles. Here, we instead harness p-phenylenediamine (PPD) as an untapped, mechanistically distinct warhead for PPL capable of labeling multiple amino acids. The reagents we introduce have higher potency (≤10 µM working concentrations) and lower background labeling than existing warheads for photosensitizers like miniSOG. To both enable multi-color PPL and further reduce background labeling, we demonstrate compatibility with deep red, genetically targetable photosensitizers such as FAP-TAPs and with multiple bioorthogonal chemistries. Proteome sequencing using a PPD probe and mitochondrial matrix-localized FAP-TAPs maintains high specificity while enriching a larger subset of the proteome not covered by existing PPL techniques.

papers.title: Trigonal Phosphine Umpolung: Electrophilicity Driven by a Redox-Active Boron Cluster
papers.abstract: Trivalent phosphines are classically defined by their nucleophilic character. The reversal of polarity, or umpolung, at phosphorus is a conceptually significant transformation leading to new reactivity. While geometrically constrained phosphines have been demonstrated to exhibit electrophilic character, similar behavior for trigonal phosphines is rare. Herein, we report direct experimental evidence of electrophilic behavior in a non-constrained trigonal phosphine enabled by the attachment of a redox-active boron cluster. The diphosphine 1-P t Bu2-2-P i Pr2closo-C2B10H10 undergoes selective addition of anionic nucleophiles, including n Bu − and CN − , at its P t Bu2 group. These reactions are accompanied by a two-electron reduction of the carborane cage and its conversion from a neutral closo-to a dianionic nido-structure, demonstrating that cluster-centered redox activity drives phosphorus-centered electrophilicity. The resulting nido-carboranyl phosphines exhibit enhanced nucleophilicity at the remaining phosphine arm, enabling subsequent trapping with alkyl halides, carbon disulfide, and electrondeficient fluoroarenes. These findings establish redox-active boron clusters as platforms for inducing umpolung and provide a new strategy for accessing ambiphilic reactivity at phosphorus.

papers.title: Systematically Improvable and Locality Accelerated Enzymatic Reactivity Modeling: Toward Chemical Accuracy at Affordable Cost
papers.abstract: Quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) is the cornerstone of computational enzymology. Herein, we address an outstanding challenge in QM/MM, namely, simultaneous access to accurate QM methodology and a large QM subsystem at an affordable computational cost. First, local natural orbital (LNO) based CCSD(T) is employed for chemically accurate energetics and references for choosing density functional theory (DFT) models. Next, reliable hybrid DFT methods are selected, with large QM subsystem selections, suitable also for reaction barriers. Then, quantum embedding, especially accelerated via our recent local embedded subsystem (LESS) approach, is used to reduce the cost of DFT calculations to a few core hours even with large QM 1 sizes up to ca. 400 QM atoms. By combining these advanced methods, we propose a Locality Accelerated (by LESS and LNO) and Systematically Improvable (LASI) scheme for QM/MM simulations. It benefits from the strengths of converged QM size in its DFT component, affordability for many configurations via quantum embedding, and, if needed, CCSD(T) accuracy for energetics. The protocol is validated through the study of challenging, representative, and clinically relevant enzyme-catalyzed phosphate hydrolysis. Based on these results, we establish generally applicable guidelines to set up the components of the LASI protocol. The flexibility and affordability of LASI, both in large scale QM or QM/MM context, make it broadly applicable for the predictive computational description of enzyme reactivity and beyond.

papers.title: The Metaproteomics Initiative: Five Years of Community-Driven Progress
papers.abstract: The Metaproteomics Initiative was officially launched in 2021 to strengthen collaboration, promote knowledge exchange, and support and lead standardization efforts within the growing metaproteomics community. Over the past five years, the Initiative has developed into a structured, global network of researchers. It has launched community-driven benchmark studies, helped shape emerging metadata and reporting standards, developed practical guidance and training materials, organized international symposia, and fostered connections across the microbiome research landscape (https://metaproteomics.org/). We outline the Initiative's organization, activities, achievements, and ongoing efforts, and reflect on how sustained, community-led coordination has shaped the development of metaproteomics as a field. We further position the Grand Metaproteome Challenges as a next step toward coordinated, community-scale biological research, aimed at advancing functional microbiome studies across clinical, industrial, and environmental application domains, and invite engagement from the wider microbiome and omics communities.

papers.title: Tips and Tricks for Organizing a Summer School -a Case Study Based on the 'Nexus of Organic Matter Analytical Developments' School
papers.abstract: Background In June 2025 we organized and ran the first 'Nexus of Organic Matter Analytical Developments' (NOMAD) Summer School at the Tjärnö Marine Laboratory in Sweden. In this article, we outline its development and implementation, with the goal of providing insight into the process, and a general framework for future events. We describe how we conceptualized the summer school and justify why it was needed, and discuss funding, advertisement, and staff and student recruitment. Additionally, we discuss how we designed the educational and social program to strike a balance between formal/informal educational and social content. In each section, we highlight what we feel went well as well as what could have been improved. There are many takeaways from the event that we think are widely applicable and will benefit other organizers seeking to develop their own summer schools. Finally, we have included student perspectives for each section written by attendees, that provide context about what participants liked and disliked regarding the structure of events like NOMAD.

papers.title: Synthonpedia -A free reaction database as a tool for retrosynthetic analysis Authors
papers.abstract: Retrosynthetic analysis represents a fundamental component of synthetic design, providing a logically consistent framework for the deconstruction of molecules of arbitrary complexity. Nevertheless, in practical applications, chemists may be influenced by cognitive biases toward well-established or familiar transformations, which can affect disconnection choices. In recent years, the rapid development of AI-driven retrosynthetic tools has sought to address these limitations by automating synthetic planning through the prediction of reaction outcomes, intermediates, and starting materials. Despite substantial advances, such approaches may still reflect biases originating from incomplete, uneven, or historically skewed literature data. Here, we introduce a new retrosynthetic tool designed to collaborate with chemists in synthesis planning. The concept is to build a freely accessible, public database of reported reactions and methodologies encoded as generalized synthon structures. Upon disconnection of a target molecule, the resulting fragments are matched against the database, and the corresponding reactions associated with the specific disconnection are retrieved. This strategy enables a systematic exploration of the reaction space covered by the database, including transformations that are infrequently reported yet may offer unconventional or insightful solutions in synthetic design.

papers.title: Impact of Sample Preparation on Chiral SFC-MS/MS Analysis of Propranolol and Its Hydroxy Metabolites in Human Urine
papers.abstract: In this study, chiral separation and mass spectrometric detection of propranolol and its hydroxy metabolites, 4',5', and 7'-hydroxypropranolol, were performed by supercritical fluid chromatography hyphenated via electrospray ionization to tandem mass spectrometry (SFC-ESI-MS/MS). Four different sample preparation methods were applied to urine samples from an excretion study after a single oral dose of 40 mg propranolol. The methods employed were dilute and inject, liquid-liquid extraction, hydrophilic-lipophilic balanced-based, and mixed-mode cation exchanger-based solid-phase extraction. For the evaluation of the sample preparation methods, the matrix effect and recovery results were taken into consideration. Furthermore, as part of extensive troubleshooting for the poor detectability of 4'hydroxypropranolol from matrix samples, post-column infusion experiments were performed, and the matrix profiles were discussed. Liquid-liquid extraction and hydrophilic-lipophilic balanced-based solidphase extraction gave the best overall results for quantitative matrix effect, recovery, and matrix profiles. Dilute and inject suffered from significant ion suppression. However, the major unsolved problem was a loss of sensitivity for signals of (R)-and (S)-4'-hydroxypropranolol.

papers.title: WITHDRAWN
papers.abstract: Withdrawn by ChemRxiv because the work was posted without approval of all co-authors.

papers.title: Stair-climbing wheelchairs for enhanced mobility: A comprehensive review of design concepts, mechanisms, and performance
papers.abstract: People with physical disabilities face significant mobility challenges while climbing uneven surfaces and staircases. In such cases, conventional wheelchairs fail to provide reliable, controlled mobility and meet the infrastructural and medical needs for highly developed stairclimbing wheelchairs. In this study, a review is proposed that provides a comprehensive summary of wheelchair types, developments, compares and evaluates existing stair-climbing wheelchair technologies, and highlights major design gaps, performance limitations, and future research directions. The review examines four fundamental categories of existing systems: tracked-based mechanisms, wheel-leg hybrid mechanisms, tri-wheel mechanisms, and automatic stair-climbing systems. These mechanisms are evaluated based on critical performance metrics, including safety and stability, ergonomics, ease of use, energy efficiency, load-carrying capacity, cost, effectiveness, adaptability to variable terrain, stair-climbing mobility performance, and control methodologies ranging from manual to AI-enabled modes. The key findings indicate that although significant advancements in stair-climbing wheelchairs have been made, current systems still face challenges in portability, weight, cost, and comfort, while recent trends highlight the growing adoption of lightweight materials, hybrid locomotion, and AI-based navigation frameworks. The proposed review has identified many research gaps, including insufficient user-centric design, high demand for low-cost, reliable real-world solutions, and the need for standardized safety testing methods for stair-climbing systems. Overall, this review will provide an overview of the different technologies and a comprehensive comparison, highlight the major design trade-offs, and suggest future research directions to advance the design and support designers, rehabilitation engineers, policymakers, and the mobility assistance technology research community in developing user-friendly, comfortable stair-climbing wheelchairs.

papers.title: Enhanced Corrosion Resistance of Next Generation Martensitic Stainless Steel for Future Energy Sector
papers.abstract: This study investigates cryogenic processing (CP), an alternative green technology, for improving corrosion resistance in energy sector applications, including fusion. CP opens the door to new tailoring options for materials used in extreme conditions by tailoring the microstructure of the materials and, consequently, their final properties, such as corrosion resistance. The resulting microstructural changes were confirmed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), X-ray diffraction (XRD), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), atom probe tomography (APT), and additional in-situ and ex-situ scanning photoelectron microscopy (SPEM) observations tailors microstructural evolution directly after its application, and later during tempering. The corrosion behaviour was tested using potentiodynamic measurements and exposure to different corrosive environments (nitrogen/oxygen atmosphere with high humidity) in scanning Kelvin probe force microscopy (SKPFM) in order to observe the growth of the passive layer and changes in surface potential. Investigating the corrosion properties and 2 microstructural features together clarifies the formation of carbides over intermetallic enrichment zones, which stabilises the microstructure. The development of next-generation metallic materials for current and future energy sectors is facilitated by this pioneering work, which provides important research for the application of CP.

papers.title: From Beach to Bulk Metal: A One-Step Self-Catalytic Hydrogen Plasma Reduction Route to Fe-Ti-V Alloys
papers.abstract: Titanomagnetite is an easily accessible and abundant Fe-rich mineral that also serves as a source for Ti and V production. However, the conventional carbon-based extraction pathways are environmentally burdensome whilst other proposed ‘green reduction’ methods are inefficient at coping with the high levels of impurities present in this complex mineralogy. Hence, new processing alternatives are needed for efficient and sustainable extraction of its constituent high-value metal elements. This study shows how sustainable hydrogen plasma smelting reduction, aided by hydrogen excited species, enables fast, efficient and selective recovery of Fe, Ti and V in a single process step and reactor. Intricate chemical partitioning occurs during the plasma reduction process that induces formation of intermediate oxide species, which then enable a form of self-catalytic enhanced oxygen exchange and removal by plasma-excited hydrogen species. As such, the process opens unconventional reduction pathways towards partial and full reduction of hard-to-reduce Ti and V-bearing oxides. These unique and innovative process-related features ultimately enable sustainable direct production of an Fe-Ti-V alloy that has the potential to mitigate 100s of Mt of CO 2 and toxic slag generation and reducing the energy intensity (4.2 GJ/t energy savings) of metal Ti and V production. Additionally, this provides the first experimental evidence to produce Ti in bulk metallic form using a hydrogen plasma, in a process that has a positive economic viability and is readily applicable to future industrial-scale deployment.

papers.title: Oxopyridine Sulfamoyl Fluorides for Covalent Bond Formation at Tyrosine and Inhibition of Ral GTPase
Mid-infrared resonant reaction in confined space driven by vibrational excitation
Thienobelts: belt-shaping thienoacenes for organic electronics
papers.abstract: Thiophene plays a fundamental role in the development of semiconducting materials for organic electronics. In this work, we introduce a novel class of thiophene-based compounds, abbreviated as thienobelts, which are obtained by wrapping up linear thienoacenes into belt-shaped structures. Ab-initio and molecular dynamics calculations are used to characterize their electronic and self-assembling properties. The results strongly suggest that thienobelts may find applications as p-type solution-processable semiconductors in the manufacture of electronic devices.

papers.title: Charge-Selective Adsorption of Organic Molecules in Microfluidic Mg(OH)2 Precipitate Membranes
papers.abstract: The porous mineral structures of alkaline hydrothermal vent chimneys have been proposed as natural concentrators of dissolved organic molecules, potentially addressing the longstanding dilution problem in deep-sea origin-of-life hypotheses. Here, we use microfluidic chemical garden precipitates composed of a primary mineral phase in white smoker chimneys, Mg(OH) 2 , to evaluate the adsorption and diffusion behavior of organic dye molecules as a function of their charge state. Pre-grown precipitate membranes are exposed to anionic (methyl orange, fluorescein), zwitterionic (rhodamine B), and cationic (crystal violet, malachite green) dye solutions under controlled flow conditions. UV-Visible spectroscopy of digested membranes reveals millimolar loading concentrations for anionic dyes after 20 h, limited uptake of the zwitterionic dye over the same period, and negligible adsorption of cationic species. Light intensity analyses of timelapse microscopy confirm that anionic dyes permeate the full membrane width within 4 h, while zwitterionic and cationic dyes remain confined near the injection interface. Steady-state and time-resolved emission measurements indicate increased environmental heterogeneity for membrane-bound fluorophores, consistent with adsorption across a distribution of pore sites. Raman and ATR-IR spectroscopy corroborate dye-mineral interactions. These results demonstrate that monomineral Mg(OH) 2 precipitates have pronounced charge-selective permeability, favoring anion transport in a manner analogous to the preferential hydroxide diffusion observed during membrane growth. This selectivity implies that negatively charged prebiotic molecules may have been preferentially concentrated within alkaline vent chimney walls, offering a mineral-mediated mechanism to locally elevate reactant concentrations in an otherwise dilute deep-sea environment.

papers.title: Charge-Selective Adsorption of Organic Molecules in Microfluidic Mg(OH)2 Precipitate Membranes
papers.abstract: The porous mineral structures of alkaline hydrothermal vent chimneys have been proposed as natural concentrators of dissolved organic molecules, potentially addressing the longstanding dilution problem in deep-sea origin-of-life hypotheses. papers.title: Virtual Screening Identifies Inhibitors and First-in-Class Activators of 17β-Hydroxysteroid Dehydrogenase Type 10
A Machine Learning Alternative to Dispersion Modeling for Estimating Near-Road Air Quality Impacts from Local to National Scales
papers.abstract: Transportation emissions are a major source of near-road air pollution in the United States, contributing to adverse health outcomes and persistent environmental inequities. Simple exposure surrogates scale easily but lack interpretability for use in health impact assessments while dispersion models provide concentration estimates at computational costs that prohibit large-scale planning and policy analysis. As a result, no common approach simultaneously achieves high spatial resolution, interpretability, and national scalability. We address this gap by creating a scalable machine learning framework that estimates ambient concentrations of primary traffic-related pollutants from small area emission density estimates. Emission density predictors are estimated on a uniform 200m grid. XGBoost regression models are then trained on high-resolution outputs from EPA's AERMOD dispersion model for six U.S. metropolitan areas to predict concentrations from the gridded emission densities. The resulting models have strong predictive performance for estimating ambient PM2.5 and NOX concentrations (R² = 0.77-0.89) and accurately reproduce near-road concentration gradients. Once trained, the framework can produce national-scale estimates at a 200m gridded resolution in several minutes, offering a practical alternative to dispersion modeling for exposure assessment, transportation planning, and policy analysis from the community to the national scale.

papers.title: Genetically encoded functionalization of liquid interfaces
papers.abstract: Surface functionalization is essential for converting otherwise inert boundaries into functional ones. Widely present in dispersed systems such as emulsions, liquid interfaces however lack the defined surface chemistry available to solid substrates, making their functionalization challenging. As a result, existing approaches remain usually top-down, complex, and highly specific to the nature of the interface or functions being introduced. Here, we propose a drastically different bottom-up, genetically encoded strategy where virtually any desired function can be brought at a wide range of liquid interfaces. It consists in cell-free expression of synthetic DNA encoding the biofilm-surface layer protein A (BslA) fused to peptides and/or proteins of interest (POIs). We demonstrate that BslA acts as a universal interfacial vector, capable of transporting and stably anchoring diverse genetically encoded POIs onto the surface of various stable oil-in-water emulsions, independent of oil type or the presence and nature of emulsifiers. Keeping the same functionalization protocol, the genetically encoded character enables to program a broad repertoire of interfacial functions such as fluorescence, on-demand protein release, specific protein recognition and capture, as well as to build droplets that can specifically bind target cells. The demonstrated robustness and versatility, combined with the breadth of encodable functionality offered by natural, engineered or de novo designed proteins, make this method a promising strategy for building customized, multifunctional soft materials.

papers.title: Local Spin Density Approximation Strongly Improved by a Better-Informed Local Scaling of its Self-Interaction Correction
FOUNDATION MODELS FOR MULTIMODAL IMAGE DATA FUSION IN MATERIALS SCIENCE
papers.abstract: This work comprehensively assesses the capabilities of recently emerging foundation models for multimodal image matching and registration in the materials science and engineering (MSE) domain. A distinctive feature in correlative materials microscopy is that the images, which need to be spatially associated, commonly not only have limited mutual information but also distinct length scales. To date, it is largely unknown how foundational multimodal matchers, such as MatchAnything RoMa or ELoFTR, which were trained predominantly with macroscale images from the human environment, generalize to image pairs in such an out-of-domain setting-especially given the pronounced information and field of view disparities in image pairs. To evaluate these models, we use the recently published AmalgaMatch dataset which covers 187 image pairs partitioned into six groups which represent distinct image matching tasks commonly faced in correlative materials microscopy and 19 subsets representing different materials. This dataset with its diverse microscopy modalities and broad range of depicted metals, alloys, and ceramics facilitates evaluation of these models in a rather representative manner. We observe that MatchAnything RoMa, as opposed to the ELoFTR variant, attains satisfactory matching results for many matching tasks and materials represented in this dataset. In contrast, image pairs within the dislocation characterization, slip partitioning and multi-scale groups pose a difficult challenge for these models. These pairs often exhibit limited mutual information and strong field of view mismatch, with field of view ratios reaching down to 2%. We propose inference strategies and workflows which embed a foundation model in an image processing pipeline to increase the matching quality and robustness and ultimately overcome aforementioned challenges inherent to MSE matching tasks.

papers.title: Tailored Multiphase Catalysis Enables Efficient Catalyst Separation and Selectivity Adaption in the Ru-Catalyzed Synthesis of Cyclic Acetals from Carbon Dioxide
papers.abstract: Herein a liquid-liquid multiphase reaction system is presented for the synthesis of cyclic acetals through the combined utilization of carbon dioxide, molecular hydrogen, and biomass-derived diols. The cationic ruthenium triphos catalyst and Lewis acid co-catalyst are immobilized in the diol substrate, while the product is recovered from the reaction phase via in situ extraction using n -decane as extraction solvent, allowing for efficient separation of catalyst and product. The multiphase approach additionally overcomes the limitation of the thermodynamic equilibrium of the acetal formation. Catalyst recycling was successfully demonstrated for ten consecutive runs, resulting in stable product formation when the byproduct water is removed after each run. The presented multiphase reaction system paves the way for the development of a continuous process for the synthesis of cyclic acetals that are increasingly interesting as sustainable fuels, solvents or monomers.

papers.title: Interplay of Catalyst and Electrode Design Governs C–C Coupling in Ag-Doped Cu Loaded Gas Diffusion Electrodes
papers.abstract: Electrochemical carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) reduction has been intensively studied as a promising route for converting CO 2 into value-added multi-carbon products such as ethylene (C 2 H 4 ). To date, most efforts have focused on the development of highly active electrocatalysts, particularly through alloying and heteroatom doping of Cu, to enhance C–C coupling and C 2 H 4 formation. However, in gas diffusion electrode (GDE) systems operated at industrially relevant current densities, CO 2 reduction proceeds at complex gas–liquid–solid triple-phase interfaces, where the structure of the catalyst layer critically governs the reaction microenvironment and product selectivity. However, how this interfacial structure affect the performance of alloyed catalysts and whether such effects can be generalized across different catalyst compositions remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that CO 2 reduction selectivity in Ag-doped Cu catalyst-loaded GDEs is governed by the cooperative interplay between catalyst and electrode design. Using Ag-doped Cu nanoparticles as a model system, we systematically investigate how Ag doping and catalyst loading collaboratively define the reaction microenvironment and CO 2 reduction selectivity. We demonstrated that moderate catalyst loadings maximize C 2 H 4 selectivity by establishing a balanced reaction environment with appropriate CO accumulation and efficient CO 2 transport, whereas excessively low or high catalyst loadings result in suppressed C 2 H 4 formation also in the alloyed catalysts. These results reveal that alloy catalyst performance is determined not only by inherent electronic and atomic properties but also by the catalyst layer configuration at the triple-phase interface. In GDE systems, optimizing this local environment is essential to fully unlock the catalysts' intrinsic activity.

papers.title: Charge Attachment Induced transport times two -sequential double-CAIT in Li3B7O12
papers.abstract: Two consecutive charge attachment induced transport (CAIT) experiments have been performed on a Li 3 B 7 O 12 glass. In the first CAIT experiment, denoted Rb + @Li 3 B 7 O 12 , Rb + ions replace native Li + ions giving rise to corresponding concentration depth profiles of Rb + and Li + . Subsequently, this ion-exchanged sample has been subjected to a second CAIT experiment where Cs + ions serve as external ions. This defines a sequential Double-CAIT experiment, here denoted Cs + @Rb + @Li 3 B 7 O 12 . Concentration depth profiles are measured by means of secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS) after the first CAIT and after the second CAIT experiment. While after the first CAIT an ion-exchange zone has formed in which the Rb + ions replace part of the native Li + ions, the concentration profile after the second CAIT reveals that Cs + was able to push Rb + and Li + ions deeper into the material. Quantitative simulation of the two concentration depth profiles by means of Nernst-Planck-Poisson theory (NPP) allows derivation of diffusion coefficients for Rb + and Li + as well as their concentration dependence. While D(Li + ) exhibits a pronounced concentration dependence in the 1st and the 2nd CAIT, D(Rb + ) appears concentration independent in the 1st CAIT but exhibits concentration dependence in the 2nd CAIT. This confirms the basic principle of CAIT, in that the external foreign ion probes the energy landscape of the sample of interest, both for a truly native as well as for an ion-exchanged sample. The results suggest that thermal equilibrium is not reached after the 1st CAIT experiment. A detailed analysis further reveals intricate ion-ion interactions connected to the similarity of bulk diffusion coefficients involved.

papers.title: Self-assembly, drug encapsulation and release properties of short amphiphilic diblock co-polymeric micelles containing different hydrophobic groups from coarse-grained simulations
papers.abstract: In the plethora of different drug carrier materials, short chain-length block co-polymers exhibit advantages such as yielding reduced lower critical solution temperatures in aqueous solutions that makes micelle formation easier. Moreover, short chains that form smaller micelle dimensions allowing advantages in penetrating the endothelial barrier. Therefore, in this work we strive to perform coarse-grained simulations of short chain-length polyethylene-glycol (PEG), polylacticacid (PLA), poly-(ε-caprolactone) (PCL), and polylactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) block copolymers to study their self-assembly, micelle properties, drug encapsulation and pH-dependent release mechanisms. The selected drugs namely, acetylsalicylic acid (ASA), ibuprofen (IBU), and gemcitabine (GEM) exhibit different levels of hydrophobicity and hydrophilicity. Our simulations show that spherical micelles can be obtained with relatively smaller sizes reaching higher encapsulation efficiency values and can release their cargo upon external stimulus following known drug release models in the literature. Developing alternative approaches to study the interactions and to understand the structure-property relationship of nanoscopic drug carriers that speed up the development process is a desired phenomenon in drug delivery field. Therefore, our findings underline the potential of small block co-polymers forming micelles can form effective drug carrier systems, and the computational approaches can be served as useful methods to understand their drug delivery properties.

papers.title: Tackling Real-World Crystal Structure Prediction from Powder X-ray Diffraction Data
papers.abstract: Crystal structure prediction (CSP) from powder diffraction data is a central challenge in materials chemistry. Machine learning (ML) models show promise, but most are trained on idealized simulated data, limiting reliability on real experiments. Here, we assess real-world behaviour using deCIFer as a representative case. deCIFer is an autoregressive transformer that conditions each step of structure generation on encoded PXRD data, guiding token-wise predictions of space group, lattice parameters, and atomic positions. Using controlled robustness tests, we quantify performance under realistic artefacts (noise, background, peak asymmetry, and Scherrer broadening) and introduce metrics for accuracy and predictive uncertainty. deCIFer adapts smoothly to signal distortions and improves over unconditioned baselines when diffraction features remain informative, while expressing appropriate uncertainty as the PXRD pattern becomes underdetermined. Tests on experimental PXRD show recovery of known structures but also highlight limitations for lower-symmetry and nanocrystalline samples. Overall, ML-based CSP is fundamentally limited by the information content of PXRD, but can accelerate expert workflows by rapidly generating chemically plausible candidates and quantifying uncertainty, making such models valuable human-in-the-loop tools for real-world structure determination.

papers.title: Multiscale Computational Discovery of an Indole-Based CK2 alpha′ Inhibitor for Huntington's Disease Therapy
Boron-mediated synthesis of phthalides
Deterministic Origin of Symmetry in Confined Water Surfaces: A Structural Approach Based on Causal Recording of Local Rules
papers.abstract: This study examines how water surface ripples evolve into spatiotemporally symmetric patterns under spatial confinement and sustained energy input. To describe this transition, this research adopt a pattern-oriented, crystallographic perspective. This research introduce physically grounded local rules that operate both internally and through boundary-driven interactions within discrete elements. Numerical simulations by this framework demonstrates that a causal recording framework can reconstruct the evolution of real water ripple patterns. In addition, validated against real-world water experiments, the results reveal that spatial confinement is a critical factor in transforming stochastic interactions into highly ordered Faraday wave-like patterns driven by local velocity heterogeneity. This research propose that this emergent regularity arises from a deterministic balance between spatial propagation limits and the superimposed interaction of regenerated forces. These findings suggest that complex fluid motion can be interpreted as an ordered registration of local force histories, providing a robust framework for understanding self-organization in confined physical systems.

papers.title: Assay-Based Machine Learning: Rethinking Evaluation in Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: The success of machine learning (ML) in drug discovery relies on modelling and evaluation strategies that accurately reflect the conditions under which compounds are tested in experimental practice. However, we found that experimental bioactivity data in public repositories like ChEMBL is highly clustered by assay origin, in both molecular structures and reported activity values. As a result, common splitting strategies, such as random or scaffold splits, still lead to more than 89\% overlap in assay origin between training and test sets across multiple ChEMBL-derived subsets. This latent overlap enables simple baselines, such as predicting the mean activity of an assay from the training data, to perform unexpectedly well on test compounds originating from the same assay. To address this issue, we propose an ML framework that accounts for the inherent structure of, especially freely available, aggregated experimental data in drug design. We implement this approach through: Evaluating our approach on three datasets derived from ChEMBL, we demonstrate that ranking models trained on intra-assay sets consistently rank compounds of unseen assays more reliably than ranking models trained on arbitrary sets and direct affinity prediction models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the correlation over the entire test set is much higher than the average correlation within experimental sets. Our findings indicate that ML methods for drug discovery should prioritize intra-assay ranking capability over absolute value prediction when working with aggregated experimental data.

papers.title: Battery Imaging Library: Multi-length scale and multi-modal synchrotron and laboratory battery imaging data for all
papers.abstract: Battery research increasingly relies on advanced imaging, yet open access to such data remains rare, scattered across various sources, and difficult to find. The Battery Imaging Library (BIL) is the first open, curated collection of multi-modal and multi-length scale battery imaging datasets, accompanied by a searchable, FAIR-compliant website. Distinctive features include the release of raw experimental data (radiographs, sinograms, X-ray and electron diffraction patterns) together with rare operando and multi-resolution datasets. Each dataset is linked to Zenodo DOIs with metadata, ensuring persistence and citability; open-source Python scripts for preprocessing and reconstruction are also provided for various CT modalities. BIL enables algorithm benchmarking, machine learning, and teaching using experimental and industrially relevant data. By combining coverage across modalities, length scales, and chemistries with raw data accessibility and a FAIR-aligned web platform, the Battery Imaging Library provides a foundation for openness and reproducibility in battery imaging. The library is available here: https://www.batteryimaginglibrary.com

papers.title: Small-data machine learning for resolving degradation challenges in energy devices
papers.abstract: Degradation is a central bottleneck for deploying next-generation energy devices, yet generating large, long-duration aging datasets is costly and slow. This perspective surveys small-data machine learning (ML) techniques that extract maximal information from limited measurements to accelerate lifetime prediction, interpretation, and optimization. Using three case studies on batteries, fuel cells, and solar cells, we benchmark feature-engineered regression models and show that simple models using carefully chosen physics-based features can forecast accurately even with small datasets. We then demonstrate how interpretable ML links processing and operating parameters to degradation pathways and how physics-informed features improve model robustness.
